Its pruned variant, PrunedDTW, optimizes DTW computation by reducing unnecessary discarding steps, thus enhancing efficiency. In this research, we introduce an enhanced PrunedDTW algorithm, referred to as Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPrunedDTW). EDPrunedDTW incorporates a previous strategy along with an elementary calculation interval size, resulting in significant computational savings. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of PrunedDTW and EDPrunedDTU: i) to achieve comparable results as DTW on a zero-risk dataset; ii) to successfully perform similarity retrieval on a dataset with real-world stock prices, employing a risk metric; and iii) to efficiently compute the nearest neighbors within a risk-optimized neighborhood size. Moreover, we provide theoretical insights on the relationships between the size of calculated intervals and the DTW distance, which, to the best of our knowledge, have not been previously established. These findings confirm that PrunedDTW and EDPrunedDTW produce statistically significant and robust results. Furthermore, PrunedDTW and EDPrunedDTW exhibit consistent and robust performance across diverse dataset risk patterns. In contrast to Early Discarding Improved Lower Bound (EDILB), PrunedDTW achieves lower computation times while producing comparable results. EDILB, on the other hand, demonstrates lower computation times than PrunedDTW but often fails to PrunedDTW's robustness. EDPrunedDTW can be seen as an EDPrunedDTW variant without early discarding, differing from EDILB but similar in terms of computation time. PrunedDTW, including its variants, represents the most efficient approach to DTW-based similarity computation, particularly early discarding PrunedDTW. Its potential applications extend beyond time series retrieval to risk-optimized PrunedDTW. EDPrunedDTW may also be utilized in various risk-based tasks. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have become a highly-preferred model for graph-based data analysis. However, such models overlook the varying importance of different graph semes when combining node features with graph semes. This oversight leads to over-blurring, a phenomenon where GCN's performance deteriorates when dealing with graphs featuring multiple semes that have been mixed together. In this context, we investigate the effect of over-blurring on GCN and explore alternative methods for improving its performance. This involves designing a new Hybrid Graph Convolution Network (HyGCN) that utilizes hybrid extra features to automatically identify usable graph semes. As a result, HyGCN surpasses state-of-the-art models in 4 out of 7 benchmark datasets, including 2 real-world applications, in a comparison that also involves 12 additional baseline methods. Furthermore, we create 7 new benchmark datasets through the hybrid extra feature mechanism and make them available for public use. This, alongside HyGCN, will be made available to address the performance limitations of existing GCN models like those seen in traditional SeGCN and GAT-GCN. This approach is expected to be beneficial in various graph-based data analysis scenarios. Additionally, a comparative study of HyGCN and 4 other top-performing models is conducted on the 6 existing benchmark datasets to highlight the general efficacy of our approach. This is accompanied by an analysis of the effect of over-blurring and a visual demonstration of HyGCN's performance using 2 real-world graph datasets. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. At the time of data collection, there were approximately 111 relevant papers. A more detailed description of the data and code is available in the repository: https://github.com/aoarang/HyGCN. Homeomorphisms with compact overlapping support on a topological space, 
denoted as $HCS(X)$, form a subgroup of the group of homeomorphisms of $X$. 
Although $HCS(X)$ is not closed in general, it contains a larger group $H_\infty(X)$. 
This group consists of homeomorphisms with support contained in a countable set of 
compact subsets of $X$. 
We show that $H_\infty(X)$ has a topological property known as local compactness, 
which implies it can be embedded in a specific type of topological group denoted as $LMC(X)$. 
The groups $HCS(X)$ and $H_\infty(X)$ share certain key characteristics, 
one of which is that they are isomorphic when $X$ is compact. 
We also define space $X$ as having'stockings' if a specific condition relating $HCS(X)$ 
and $H_\infty(X)$ is met. 
One key result is that if $X$ has stockinged homotopy type to a compact space $Y$, 
then $LMC(X)$ and $LMC(Y)$ are topologically equivalent. 
This concept extends to a category known as Space with Stockings, for which a diaphragm exists, 
along with an analogue of the fundamental group called the fundamental stockinged group. 
We also show that if $X$ and $Y$ are spaces with stockinged homotopy type to each other, 
their corresponding generalized homotopy groups are topologically equivalent.

denoted as $LMC(\mathfr{C})$.

along with its corresponding group structure, showing that it satisfies the properties of a group,

Research into remote epitaxy on graphene layers is gaining momentum as a means to bypass the substrate lattice match requirement, a hallmark characteristic of the process.  However, achieving successful epitaxy through this approach poses a significant challenge.  This study involves the epitaxial growth of the Heusler alloy series on graphene-coated sapphire substrates.  Three distinct remote epitaxy mechanisms - involving pinholes, van der Waals epitaxy, and solid-phase epitaxy - compete during the growth process. In contemporary information seeking, a query is typically entered into a search engine, yielding a vast list of items, often spanning hundreds of thousands. In contrast, our study reframes information seeking as a dialogue between a seeker and an informant, akin to a knowledgeable friend providing personalized guidance. We have devised a set of 38 seeker profiles, each characterized by their information needs, to demonstrate how a more detailed understanding of seekers' identities can inform tailored, 'knowledgeable friend'-style counseling. These seeker profiles, originally based on empirical research, have been revised to better match real-world seeking behaviors. We have also developed a corresponding list of counselor responses, acting as an 'knowledgeable friend', to guide seekers through a sequential problem-solving process. Through this structured approach, we aim to bridge the gap between information seeking research and the 'knowledgeable friend' counseling method. We now explore how seeker profiles, incorporating seeking behaviors, can be utilized to provide comprehensive, contextualized counseling in the manner of a personal guide. We plan to expand upon this framework, increasing the number of seeker profiles and counselor responses, to establish a comprehensive library of seeking behaviors and related counseling strategies. This library can serve as an accessible, contextualized reference point for researchers and practitioners. Recent advancements in deep learning have been successfully applied to diagnose ADHD using fMRI data, focusing primarily on identifying essential features to distinguish between ADHD and control groups. Despite the high dependency of these methods on crucial brain regions, which are not universally agreed upon, many studies have relied on feed-forward neural networks. As a result, trying to identify the most critical areas of the brain involved in ADHD diagnosis has become a pressing concern. In order to address this challenge, we examined various ADHD diagnosis models, asking which brain regions these networks were concentrating on and whether involving a motor control area, previously linked to ADHD, would improve diagnostic accuracy. Employing rs-fMRI data from the ADHD 200 dataset and an ensemble of convolutional neural networks, we tested the hypothesis that including additional right frontal regions would enhance classification performance. Experimental results showed that by including right frontal regions in the diagnosis model, the ensemble achieved a 2% improvement in accuracy compared to models relying solely on baseline regions. Notably, the ensemble outperformed individual network components by 10%, highlighting the significance of right frontal regions for ADHD diagnosis. Furthermore, mappings of the most active slices across various models revealed the potential of right frontal regions to facilitate the diagnosis. Our study's findings suggest that right frontal regions, involving the premotor area, are crucial for enhancing deep learning-based ADHD diagnosis. The diagnostic model's increased accuracy when right frontal regions were involved indicated that these areas were essential for successfully training deep learning models to diagnose ADHD. Quantum interference, a crucial phenomenon governing quantum transport, is often seen in interaction-driven systems. We investigate its impact on the transport characteristics of a specific nanoscale circuit, comprising two quantum Hall bars connected by a point contact, where interactions between electrons cause thermoelectric effects and heat transfer. These thermoelectric properties can be controlled through phase-sensitive interference by applying an external electric field that acts as a switch. At the quantum scale, this system exhibits distinct behaviors, particularly heat rectification and a phenomenon known as thermally mediated electrical entanglement. Our study also explores the interplay between quantum interference and interactions in determining thermoelectric properties. As experiments using quantum Hall systems are feasible, our findings could be verified through careful observation. We have also developed a corresponding setup for studying the related heat transfer using a quantum Monte Carlo simulation. Our analysis reveals an intricate connection between heat and charge transport, illustrating how thermoelectric effects facilitate the conversion of heat into electrical energy and vice versa. These findings can be valuable in designing novel thermoelectric devices that harness these interactions effectively. Our study also identifies potential signs of thermoelectric turbulence, which could arise due to interactions, for future investigation. Our proposed solution leverages a hierarchical data organization strategy to expedite access to frequently requested data in DNA storage systems. To achieve this, we develop a recursive placement strategy that allocates segments of DNA sequences according to a pre-determined hierarchy. When a read request occurs, we simulate the time taken to retrieve the associated base pairs and calculate the optimal extraction strategy to minimize the number of seals needed, thereby reducing the time and temperature requirements. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of utilizing ancillary strands for data refreshes, allowing for the simultaneous retrieval of multiple data segments upon the breaking of a single seal. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can attain a data refresh rate 3.91x higher than that of a random placement strategy, while also achieving a 2.19x higher retrieval rate than that of a sequential extraction strategy. Additionally, we identify potential limitations and challenges associated with our solution, encompassing the need for enhanced DNA writing speeds, the development of more sophisticated DNA sliders, as well as the creation of tools for measuring the thermal conductivity of DNA. Our work on hierarchical data organization is contributed as an open-source feature to the CDS tool framework. It enables researchers to conduct performance assessments based on their individual storage requirements. To facilitate this, we establish a comprehensive benchmarking suite that includes workloads from areas like file system access, YouTube video storage, and web indexing. Our findings reveal that hierarchical data organization can enhance data retrieval rates by as much as 1.53x and expedite data refreshes by as much as 3.91x. Moreover, we explore the theoretical limitations of our approach, encompassing the efficiency gain cap of 4.25x and the minimum 1.92% error rate for data extraction, both of which are dictated by the properties of the double helix structure. To assist researchers in applying the hierarchical data organization strategy, we establish two code bases: an open-source CDS feature and the CDS-HO tool, both of which are freely accessible under the terms of the BSD-3 license. Momentum-space nodal surfaces, present in momentum eigenstates of certain operators, exhibit a topological invariance, leading to partially protected rules regarding their occurrence in combined systems. This rule has been successfully applied to design photonic devices, including isolators and switches, by leveraging photonic quantum wells with designed potentials. Recent research has further adapted this approach using coupled waveguide systems with specially engineered couplings. This progress has potentially enabled the development of momentum-space topological photonic devices, including momentum-controlled switches and filters. However, the underlying physics of these systems remains complex and requires detailed analysis. This concept review discusses the theoretical background of momentum-space nodal surfaces and their implementation in recent photonic and other devices, providing a thorough understanding of the underlying principles. It begins by explaining the momentum-space nodal surfaces and their topological invariances before discussing recent implementations using photonic and other systems, ultimately concluding with an examination of the underlying physics. In oscillatory networks of chemical reactions, pacemaker-generated waves exhibit a unique characteristic, where a region of autonomous autocatalytic reaction generates periodic output. We examined the velocity of these waves in two models. In the first model based on the Landel-Douda reaction, we identified the velocity as a sum of contributions from the boundary and interior regions. We obtained analytical estimates for the velocity in both the weak and intermediate regimes. In the second model based on the Briggs-Rauscher reaction, we employed a hydrodynamic approach and applied the method of matched asymptotic expansions to find the velocity's leading-order approximation. We verified our analytical estimates through numerical simulation and compared them to each other, as well as to previous numerical results. Furthermore, we observed the impact of changing parameters on the velocity's behavior. We discovered that in both models the velocity exhibits auto-sustable behavior, where it may increase or decrease depending on parameter values. In addition, we found similar velocity dynamics between the two models despite differing mechanisms, which suggests a common underlying universal behavior. We also explored the applications and possibilities for which these analytical estimates could be useful. We propose these estimates as a potential alternative to numerical methods for determining wave velocities in intricate networks of chemical reactions. The possible extensions of these findings to biologic processes are also discussed. We also suggest the use of these analytical estimates in conjunction with other numerical and analytical methods for a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms. In particular, we propose these estimates as a potential tool for the verification of simulation and modeling results. A novel quantum learning algorithm known as the Quantum Walk algorithm has been developed for identifying patterns in datasets with binary outcomes. When applied to a quantum system lacking measurements, the algorithm induces a controlled evolution that enables a trained quantum circuit to emerge from a pre-defined one. This occurrence is not influenced by random fluctuations. Furthermore, the algorithm can be represented using a quantum circuit comprising a series of rotations and the application of X-gates, established the relationship between learning and solutions to Lam\'{e} equations. Experimentally, the algorithm was evaluated on superconducting quantum processors, which were shown to exhibit an advantage when compared to their classical counterparts for data sizes of 2^9 and 2^10. Our findings indicate that the learning process is significantly accelerated when instructed, whereas the learning process that occurs without instruction exhibits an exponential relationship with the dataset size. This study marks the first real-world demonstration of the Quantum Walk algorithm on superconducting processors, and the results suggest the potential for a quantum advantage in machine learning applications. The research also identifies areas for improving the results, such as enhancing circuit fidelity through the development of new multi-qubit gates. Finally, the findings present an opportunity to explore the potential of quantum circuits to learn, and the relationship between this ability and the existence of additional qubits. Our anomalous microlensing follow-up program with the KMTNet network has entered its fifth phase, where we analyzed all 2018 microlensing phenomena from the KMTNet Archive. From a total of 86 selected targets with suitable data, 50 entered our final review process and 28 of those met the criteria for this study. It's noteworthy that 20 of these 28 were found to have celestial anomalies consistent with a macrophotometry technique called the Gaussian Amplitude Wing technique, where 11 showed characteristic "X" shapes and 9 exhibited "S" shapes. Additionally, 9 of these 28 exhibited anomalies according to the differential signal preservation method. To further confirm the cause of these anomalies, we examined the underlying telescope data and found that bad weather, gear issues, and data quality problems could produce the characteristic X-shapes, while the S-shapes were found to be influenced by the focal plane microlensing zone's position and also by gear problems. Finally, we speculate that the cause of the anomalies is likely attributed to the main factors being of an instrumental nature. Our study is the most comprehensive to date on the topic, having analyzed 86 targets, whereas previous studies looked at 42 from 2015 and 49 from 2016. Our findings also include specific equations that help distinguish celestial anomalies from microlensing signals, allowing for the identification of such anomalies in the KMTNet archive using a simplified method. Our study is significant as it may contribute to the detection of additional small telescopes that enable gravitational microlensing planets' identification. Differentiable rendering has emerged as a highly favorable approach towards solving inverse problems in computer vision, due to its capacity to model forward image formation processes in an analytically predictable manner. However, research in this area has been hindered by the non-differentiable nature of traditional rendering methods, specifically volume rendering and shadow calculation. In this study, we present novel differentiable algorithms for these two imaging components, thereby enriching the differential rendering toolkit and making a significant contribution to the field. Our method for computing shadows, in particular, generalizes to handle the rendering of multi-layered radiance fields, a concept recently introduced by Liu et al. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms. The code for these algorithms has been made publicly available. For the volume rendering component, we refer the reader to Chen et al.'s signed depth buffer, and for the shadow calculation component, we present an alternative method. Our contribution for volume rendering is trivial, as we simply apply signed depth buffers, whereas our contribution for shadow calculation is significant, as we derive a differentiable formula for calculating shadows, even for objects with intricate geometric details and an infinite number of layers, without being confined to basic spherical shapes. Our method also allows for the use of pre-rendered volume images, thereby rendering the volume rendering process differentiable. A publicly accessible JAX-based implementation of our method has been made available. In addition to this implementation, we have created a series of publically accessible training datasets, comprising 64,000 images, along with their corresponding differentiable pixel masks, a set of 4,000 image pairs, and corresponding sparse view data for scene inference. These datasets can be accessed at: https://github.com/aminabadi/dsrs/blob/main/data.zip. The proposed algorithm has been evaluated on three benchmarking datasets, comprising (i) real-world car data, (ii) synthetic rooms, and (iii) 3D characters. Results have been obtained using a Google V2 GPU. Transportation managers face the challenge of determining origin-destination demand probabilities for multiple days with limited information. Typically, a small set of samples from origin-destination matrices, along with the day-to-day consistency of traffic patterns, are known. This paper develops a mathematical framework for estimating origin-destination demand probability distributions that maximize day-to-day consistency while adhering to the constraints imposed by the available traffic data. Our approach is similar to classical statistical estimation methods but incorporates the unique characteristics of matrix data and day-to-day consistency, yielding a unique distribution known as the Type-II Generalized Gamma distribution. We provide closed-form solutions for parameter estimation and demonstrate their effectiveness using a case study. Our proposal has the advantage of producing a single, stable solution rather than relying on iterative methods or assuming parameters to be known or zero. Furthermore, our approach enables the computation of margin of error and performance measures such as accuracy, relative bias, and coverage, thereby providing a comprehensive evaluation of our solution. In addition, our case study highlights the importance of day-to-day consistency in origin-destination demand probability distributions, illustrating cases where the two characteristics are mutually dependent and independent. Our proposed method can be applied to a wide range of statistical estimation problems involving matrices, including the estimation of link demand distributions and network flow patterns. Our work offers a comprehensive framework for origin-destination demand probability distribution estimation that meets the demands of both transportation managers and researchers, addressing concerns such as readability, clarity, and content. Our proposal has been made available as a software library, named DistrCalc, for matrix distribution calculation, allowing for rapid computation of origin-destination demand probability distributions. DistrCalc is designed to be a user-friendly, interactive tool that is aware of existing literature and provides a comprehensive overview of distribution calculation, including Type-II Generalized Gamma, Gamma, Lognormal, and Uniform distributions. Our approach also incorporates features such as distribution evaluation, sensitivity analysis, and sensitivity scaling. Moreover, DistrCalc synergizes with existing traffic software to provide a comprehensive workflow, exemplified by our case study, where we employed DistrCalc in conjunction with ITS-Denver software to obtain accurate origin-destination demand probability distributions that also passed validation tests and were scaled for sensitivity. Our software library, DistrCalc, has been made available online, allowing for a wide range of applications. Our work has also sparked new research questions, particularly the effect of day-to-day consistency on origin-destination demand probability distributions, and whether day-to-day consistency is inherent in traffic data. In interdependent systems, a tiny disturbance can spread quickly through a network, impacting various components and potentially leading to a cascade of failures. This concept applies to biological processes such as coordinated movement in insects and the regulation of heartbeats in animals. Researchers have created a model consisting of an array of nonlinear oscillators connected through links of different strengths to study synchronized behavior in complex networks. By manipulating the strength and number of connections between oscillators, they have discovered phases in the system where some oscillators are actively connected, while others are disconnected. This is in contrast to traditional models, which suggest that oscillators within a cluster are equally connected and move in unison. Furthermore, the system was subjected to external influences, such as weakening and adding new connections, which can shift the phase and potentially lead to oscillator synchrony across different clusters. This approach provides a potential framework for understanding and analyzing the delicate balance of biological systems that facilitate coordinated movements and other complex tasks. It also offers a potential method for designing self-organizing systems that facilitate distributed, coordinated activity. The study used an array of nonlinear oscillator models, including examples inspired by fundaments of mechanics and electrical circuits, as well as more complex systems with inherent time delays. By manipulating the phase and connecting different oscillators, they have discovered diverse stable states and pathways to failure, and found similarities and differences between the various systems, dependent on their underlying dynamics. The research has also led to the design of an experiment that the team carried out using an array of specialized, light-sensitive oscillators that they had built. The study's findings have broader applications, including the understanding of insect migration patterns and the design of self-organizing technologies. In addition, the research has the potential to contribute to the analysis of biological systems that rely on coordinated movements, such as the navigation of fish schools and the regulation of heartbeats in animals. The research has also identified connections between the underlying dynamics of the oscillator model and the design of frequency control systems. Lastly, the research has the potential to facilitate the analysis of the delicate balance of biological systems that facilitate coordinated movements and other complex tasks. This realization led to the development of a two-phase approach for generating uniform spanning trees, incorporating elements of both algorithms. This new framework offers potential enhancements and simplifications for tree generation, potentially improving random graph exploration and other related algorithms. This research explores enhancing user understanding of complex datasets, leveraging the power of natural language processing's word embeddings. We have developed two applications - Ontodia Viewer and Wikidata Entity Viewer - to visualize data, which are discussed below.

Initially, we examined how users study visual information and identified two primary methods: utilizing questions and creating notes. We developed two methods to facilitate this investigation: (1) capturing and annotating entities found in highlights or questions from Wikidata and Ontodia projects, (2) creating an interactive timeline to display user-created annotations in the order they were made. Word embeddings are then used to analyze these annotations and suggest relevant entities based on their semantic connections.

Furthermore, we developed the Ontodia Viewer and Wikidata Entity Viewer, integrating them with the Ontodia and Wikidata APIs to enable exploration. We have made these applications open-source and plan to make the source code available under the MIT license. We believe this combination of visualization and NLP, coupled with the open-source nature of our tools, offers significant potential for data investigation. We illustrate the capabilities of these tools using case studies on topics like 'Countries with the most visited attractions' and 'Characteristics of Schenectady cities'. We have also conducted preliminary experiments to gauge the understanding of the generated suggestions. We aim to build upon these results, providing more substantial evaluations in the future.

The problem of solving an elastic-inelastic combined heart model involves multiple right-hand sides and can benefit from employing multilevel solvers due to their capability to exploit problem structure and reduce memory consumption. A particular multilevel solver called MLUPLO is shown to be effective in this context, demonstrating superior performance in weak scaling tests compared to other popular multilevel solvers like MLUPLO's competitors in UPAI. MLUPLO's performance advantage arises from its ability to efficiently handle problem variation through the use of an interface problem solver and a preconditioner that effectively exploits problem sub-decomposition, including the application of elastic-inelastic boundary condition solvers. Furthermore, MLUPLO's design facilitates easy implementation of additional components such as non-linear solver modifiers and post-processing tools. MLUPLO's capabilities are further demonstrated through its successful simulation of a minute of cardiac cycle dynamics, showcasing the importance of incorporating both elastic and inertial mechanical components. MLUPLO's performance is made to compare with PARDISO, a high-performance direct solver optimized for many-core architectures, to evaluate its impact on large-scale heart model simulations. We investigate the long-term behavior of solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model with physical boundaries and coordinate-independent molecular alignment. Utilizing a global-in-time solver for the associated evolution equation of the alignment tensor, we demonstrate that any globally smooth solution remains controlled and, furthermore, its characteristic sizes do not change over time in the case of mild initial data. This allows us to establish a key estimate for the long-term behavior of solutions with physically realistic initial conditions. We show that solutions with physically realistic initial conditions are uniformly controlled and, in addition, the long-term behavior of solutions with different viscoelasticity parameters converges to a specific solution with the extreme viscoelasticity parameter. This conclusion is consistent with numerical simulation results presented in the paper. To confirm that the obtained uniform bounds are the best possible, we demonstrate that solutions with extremely different initial conditions cannot approach each other in a certain metric. We also provide further support for the results via additional numerical simulation results. Moreover, we extend the obtained bounds to solutions that are not smooth, but rather have limited smoothness, by employing a specific estimate for the alignment tensor. The estimate is derived by applying various techniques, including a generalization of a priori estimate for the alignment tensor, the nature of which is not straightforward, as well as the use of little-Leray estimates for the velocity gradient. We use a special approach to close the estimation chain and, in doing so, reveal the underlying structure of the model, showing that certain terms are not dissipative. We also apply a special technique to estimate the movement of locations where the alignment tensor values are zero. The technique is grounded in the use of a special formula that describes the time change of the area of a specific region. We use an alternative method to estimate the movement of locations where the alignment tensor values are zero that is grounded in the use of a specific flow characteristic. We also use a special priori estimate that involves the alignment tensor and its gradient. The estimate is of particular interest because it is the first such estimate for the alignment tensor and its gradient and confirms the expected nature of the alignment tensor. We also apply a special flow characteristic to confirm the expected nature of the rotation tensor and its gradient. The expected nature was previously the subject of debate. We also use an alternative method, grounded in the use of a special flow characteristic, to confirm the expected nature of the rotation tensor and its gradient. The expected nature was previously the subject of debate. We also provide further support for the results via additional numerical simulation results

Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through wireless connections offers a promising approach to developing flexible and cost-effective network configurations. Mobile IAB, which facilitates the connection to the user, is particularly appealing as it enables a mix of fixed and mobile IAB nodes within a network. In this paper, we explore the IAB convergence process, focusing on mobile IAB and examining the key issues, proposed solutions, and challenges associated with it. The key areas of discussion include diversity techniques, channel acquisition methods, adaptive IAB routing, channel allocation strategies, QoS provision, and cross-layer IAB approaches. The IAB standardization process and the complexities involved in deploying a mobile IAB network are also discussed. The IAB performance in different scenarios is evaluated using simulation, which shows that IAB outperforms other networking approaches in terms of total link utilization and user data transmission rate. The IAB values of these performance metrics are 30.64 dB and 0.22 bits/s/J, respectively. Furthermore, we examine the IAB time-dependent characteristics, specifically the correlation dimension and exponent, which help in understanding the IAB time-response function. The IAB correlation exponent quantifies the IAB time-response behavior, ranging from stochastic (exponent value: 2) to deterministic (exponent value: 2.4). The IAB correlation exponent assessment enables the IAB time-response prediction accuracy (95%) and the IAB modeling simplicity (measured in bits). The IAB correlation exponent of mobile IAB nodes exhibits higher values than those of fixed IAB nodes, which indicates more accurate IAB time-response prediction and simpler IAB models for mobile IAB nodes. The IAB correlation exponent of mobile IAB nodes also exhibits dependence on the IAB node speed (measured in meters/second) and the IAB channel bandwidth (measured in bits/meter/second), which enables the IAB time-response prediction and the IAB model simplification based on these parameters. The IAB standard, which outlines the IAB channel allocation rules, also depends on the IAB node distance (measured in meters), the IAB node direction (measured in radians), the IAB node speed, and the IAB channel bandwidth. The IAB standard supports the IAB channel allocation for single- and multi-row IAB networks, featuring one to four IAB rows and various IAB channel allocation rules. The IAB standard evaluates the IAB channel allocation performance in terms of total link utilization and user data transmission rate

For decades, finding the optimal settings for hyperparameters in machine learning algorithms has been a challenging problem. This study applies global sensitivity analysis to the issue of determining effective hyperparameters for fitness functions, and in this paper, we focus on the fitness functions of reinforcement learning. The authors examine the relative importance of 11 hyperparameters from the Rastrigin function using Sobol's method and propose an affordable alternative, the forward partial variance algorithm. The results indicate that the optimal number of generations is the most sensitive parameter for this fitness function. This research also investigates the anisotropic sensitivity of 14 hyperparameters for 4 benchmark functions and finds that the scale parameter is the most influential for the Rastrigin function. The results suggest that optimizing the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of a multivariate normal distribution could improve the results of evolutionary algorithms. This study aims to provide a framework for evaluating the efficacy of hyperparameters for fitness functions, and in this paper, we restrict our analysis to stationary fitness functions but plan to explore the dynamics of fitness functions in future work. The authors suggest considering more sensitive parameters first and implementing global sensitivity analysis early in the development stage of algorithms to inform design decisions. This study also finds that there is no universally optimal set of hyperparameters for benchmark functions, and therefore, global sensitivity analysis should be used in conjunction with other methods to guide algorithmic design. The authors further suggest conducting sensitivity analysis on specific problems rather than benchmark functions and that this study constitutes a theoretical contribution to the field. The results of this study are available in an online library. The authors implemented their analysis using Python 3 with the PySTA library and provide the code as a guide for researchers. This study was motivated by the authors' experience working on projects in the field of reinforcement learning and fitness functions. The authors believe that global sensitivity analysis can be applied to other fields such as optimization, regression, and classification, and that this study constitutes a real-world example of its application. The results of this study are consistent with previous findings and the authors aim to facilitate future research in this area. The authors also examine the robustness of fitness functions and plan to explore this topic in future work. The proposed method could be used to guide the development of algorithms for solving specific problems, and the authors provide a framework for evaluating the efficacy of hyperparameters. The results of this study are multi-faceted and provide guidance on the relative importance of parameters for evaluating fitness functions. The authors aim to apply this study to the field of reinforcement learning and provide a concrete example of its application

The mathematical structure of the wave equation serves as a precursor to quantum theory, ultimately leading to the widespread adoption of wave functions as the central element of quantum theory. The linear Schrödinger equation played a key role in the early 20th century in establishing quantum theory, albeit with much debate surrounding non-linear variants of the wave equation. This article explores three specific areas of discussion: first, the relationship between wave functions and probability distributions; second, interpretations of the wave function, specifically focusing on the unique predictions offered by wave function collapse models; and third, potential applications of nonlinear Schrödinger equations in modeling physical systems, drawing on a recent example involving wave function splitting. We hope that these debates will stimulate further research into nonlinear wave equations and their potential solutions to longstanding problems in quantum theory. In particular, the discussion centers on the probabilistic nature of wave functions and the differing interpretations among physicists, specifically the dynamical wave function collapse theory and its unique predictions. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in real-world contexts, such as changing environments or shifting user preferences in recommendations. In particular, the challenge of retaining learning capabilities in the face of continually expanding domains poses a substantial obstacle. To address this, lifelong reinforcement learning (LRL) has emerged as a promising framework, but evaluating its effectiveness is complicated by the need to custom-design tasks for precise experimental purposes. To overcome this limitation, we introduce $L2Explorer$, an open-source, versatile platform that enables flexible construction of LRL tasks across diverse domains, including recommendation systems, multi-scale search, and others. This framework can be configured to mimic a range of real-world scenarios through its built-in features, including dynamic domain expansion, shifting reward functions, and explicit memory. Our benchmarking approach for LRL task design emphasizes robustness, scalability, and ease of implementation to allow for thorough evaluations of existing methods as well as the development of new strategies to tackle complex LRL challenges. Furthermore, $L2Explorer$'s design also addresses the lack of open-source, continuous-action evaluation environments, making it a useful resource for the reinforcement learning community. This framework is expected to spur future research by enabling thorough evaluations of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. You can find the code and additional information at https://github.com/learn2learn/L2Explorer. Supplemental materials are available at https://l2x.github.io/L2Explorer. This work is inspired by the discussion during the lancutME workshop on lifelong reinforcement learning, held during IJCAI 2021. $\mathbf{This\ paper\ is\ made\ possible\ by\ the\ grant\ #\ INE-62020A}$ from the government. The underlying data for this work can be found under the identifier https://doi.org/10.6084/m1e.urn:ghent:202310T220236.

This study uncovers a novel family of highly irregular and accelerating waves that emerge near a standard 2D Couette flow in the Euler equation. These high-speed waves originate from the intersection of two distinct stationary vortex structures, forming a singular event. Furthermore, we demonstrate that as these waves accelerate, their associated surface in the phase space converges at a finite distance, while their vorticity distribution exhibits oscillations between two stationary states. Notably, we find that the maximum speed of these waves is determined by the average of their minimum and maximum asymptotic velocities, a phenomenon that holds for any 2D Quasilinear Euler equation. An analytical model is also developed to explain the irregular behavior of these waves at very high speeds. An interesting observation is that the maximum speed of these waves is comparable to that of another fast-moving wave type identified near a different 2D equilibrium state, known as the geostrophic equilibrium. An intriguing connection is then proposed between these waves and those observed in the geostrophic equilibrium context. An extension of our models that takes into account the effects of viscosity yields the existence of an irreversible transition, supporting the idea that the irreversible behavior of these waves may be a natural, reversible phenomenon that is observable in the irreversible flow context. An essential question arises as to whether it is possible to generalize the wave types identified in this study to other 2D equilibrium states beyond Couette flow and the geostrophic equilibrium. An important area for future research is the identification of additional wave types and the development of a comprehensive classification system that can encompass all possible wave types in both the reversible and irreversible flow contexts. Additionally, we point out the possibility that the types of waves identified in this study may be observable in certain types of liquids, as well as airplanes, helicopters, and other types of rotating machines. Upon conducting an online search, we found that the behavior of these waves appears to be consistent with the observations of fluid dynamics experts, as well as pilots and other professionals. The COVID-19 pandemic, categorised as a global health crisis by the WHO, has resulted in severe economic and societal repercussions. To combat this outbreak, governments have implemented stringent control measures, aiming to balance crisis mitigation with minimal economic impact. To make informed decisions, accurate and frequently updated data are essential; however, the infrastructure to collect and analyse this data may be limited during emergencies. To fill this gap, we examined publicly accessible data in South Africa, including time-stamped geo-location information from mobile network data, as a potential alternative to inform critical policy decisions during the COVID-19 epidemic. By analysing this data with statistical and machine learning methods, we identified patterns and predictions that align with official reported cases, demonstrating its informative value. Furthermore, we analysed the mobility trends of South Africans, observing reduced movement in February, followed by varying degrees of decrease in different provinces. Our findings indicate that mobile network data can effectively inform crisis decision-making, despite inherent biases. To facilitate data-driven decision-making during emergencies, we suggest integrating data analysis frameworks that leverage accessible data, such as mobile network data, to inform critical policy decisions. The code used in this study is publicly accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/husseiny/COVID-19/tree/main-South_Africa. The data visualisations are available online at https://github.com/husseiny/COVID-19/tree/main-South_Africavisualizations. This research is based on a completed project that was submitted to GSoC-2020 under the supervision of Dr. Leana A. Bouwe van Dunem and Dr. husseiny. We officially submitted our work to arXiv on July 26, 2021. We have since made the associated resources publicly accessible as per the CC-BY license terms. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In essence, this theorem reveals that any two subsets of integers, of a similar size to their sumset, necessarily resemble arithmetic progressions. Our analysis provides an enhanced version of this theorem, applicable in instances where the sumset's size is merely above 2k. We based our proof on an iterative procedure, splitting the first k elements into potential arithmetic progressions, analyzing their overlaps, and applying a generalized version of the Balog-Szemer\'edi Green-Tao theorem. We expect this enhanced theorem to have far-reaching implications in additive combinatorics. Moreover, we rely on a key argument originating from the preprint 'Freiman's theorem for groups with applications to 'ruptly large subgroups' by Ben Green, and also draw parallels with a recent contribution by Allen and Ruzsa. We have further supplemented the theorem with an explicit example, showcasing two dense subsets of integers that are near arithmetic progressions, yet fail to exhibit any noticeable similarity to arithmetic progressions. We note that our analysis directly yields an improved version of a theorem recently independent by Martin Ranson. We have also applied our enhanced version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem to demonstrate an analytical solution to a long-standing diophantine problem, inquiring about the existence of two dense, submonoid-based, arithmetic progression families, whose sumsets reach almost double their combined sizes. In medical research, incorporating multiple data types has become a standard approach to addressing complex tasks. This method has been successfully applied to the visual system and is now being explored for the diagnosis and monitoring of ocular disorders such as glaucoma and age-related macular degeneration. A recent study investigated the effectiveness of combining two modalities - retinal image and clinical data - for classifying diseases. This study evaluated various data integration techniques and proposed a novel approach that prioritizes modality specializations to improve classification accuracy. The findings also investigated the impact of excluding individual modalities on the performance of the integrated model. The researchers further analyzed the integrated model's performance when certain modalities were removed and identified that, although including all modalities yielded the best results, removing the least contributing modality (clinical data) slightly improved the integrated model's performance without significantly compromising its reliability. The integrated model showed a significant improvement in classification accuracy when including all available data compared to single-modality approaches. The findings suggest that multidimensional data integration can lead to more accurate outcomes and should be considered a reliable classification method. X-ray images have been widely used in COVID-19 research, with many studies relying on machine learning models to identify critical characteristics from these images. Although some studies have focused on hospitalization conditions, there is a lack of information on the relationship between X-ray image features and ICU admission requirements. In this study, we investigated six possible characteristics of ICU admission through a transfer learning approach on a large dataset of COVID-19 cases. By evaluating these characteristics, clinicians can gain more insight into the progression of the disease and make more informed decisions when treating patients. Furthermore, this knowledge can be utilized to develop AI systems that take clinical standards into account when making decisions. With this in mind, we aimed to identify the features of ICU admission and assess their reliability in a real-world context. Additionally, we conducted ethically aware AI development, considering aspects such as patient data protection and model explainability. The results of our research are available online for others to build upon. With rapidly evolving COVID-19 data, we plan to update our findings regularly to reflect any changes and collaborate with other researchers who may share the same goals. Image classification is a fundamental task in computer vision, a core function of the human visual system. Previous research has shown that neural networks can accurately perform image classification, but these methods rely on pre-defined labels for training, assuming label reciprocity and symmetry. In contrast, our study focuses on multi-object recognition, where interactions and relationships between objects are inherent parts of the task. To better capture these interactions, we introduce the Active Graph Message Transfer network (AGMT), a neural network that grounds objects in a scene spatially and visually. Through directed relationships, objects can be linked as actors, targets, or in other roles, describing how they interact. Our proposed AGMT is an end-to-end trainable neural network that learns to recognize objects in a scene through their interactions. By modeling the graph over images using spatial and channel attention, the network can capture complex multi-object interactions and predict the primary target based on the action it receives. Through experiments, the proposed AGMT achieved superior performance on multi-object datasets, outperforming baseline models by 25.5, 11.6, and 8.3 percent on the PASCAL Context, NUS-WIDE, and ImageNet-30-Scene datasets. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/philcrump/ActiveGraphMessageTransfer. Our method demonstrates that multi-object recognition can be achieved through interactions and is a step towards simulating how the human visual system recognizes and interacts with objects in a scene. Additionally, the proposed AGMT is an end-to-end neural network that learns to recognize objects based on their interactions, showing promise for future research in simulating the complex interactions of the human visual system. To demonstrate the capabilities of our method, we created a multi-object recognition task where the target is not among the initial objects, requiring the network to predict it based on the action and interactions provided. The target was chosen randomly as the primary object in the scene, with the network achieving a 71.4 percent accuracy rate on this challenging task. The proposed AGMT is a significant advancement in multi-object recognition, demonstrating through directed relationships how objects interact in a scene and accurately predicting the primary target based on these interactions and the action it receives. According to the standard model of cosmology, the density of such black holes should be in proportion to $1/m^2$ where $m$ represents their mass. This research introduces the Virtual Protected Framework, a modern processor architecture specifically designed to process VPP instructions and optimize the execution of Side Channel Attack resistant programs. Building on the foundation laid by van Dijk et al. in 2012, we enhance and simplify the existing four-stage pipeline with five stages, overwinding previous work on protected gate and partial evaluation. Our design, incorporating a novel five-stage Integer Arithmetic Logic Unit, enables Self-Correcting Execution and preserves complete program integrity. Moreover, the VPF follows a True Prime Homomorphic Encryption architecture, facilitating secure and compatible communication between compatible programs. Our numerical evaluation demonstrates that the VPF, despite its additional overhead, can still match or exceed the performance of the original programs, while fundamentally protecting programs against Side Channel Attacks. All our results are substantiated by both theoretical and practical analyses. This research has been influenced by real-world programs, which we then apply to an HE-based processor, thereby contributing to the field in a meaningful way. This research is part of a broader effort to extend Processor Architecture to include Side Channel Attack resistance as a fundamental component, thus promoting the development of more trustworthy software and protecting valuable intellectual property. This research is distinct from previous efforts, which have often focused on developing software countermeasures; in contrast, we introduce a processor architecture that incorporates protection mechanisms, thereby facilitating the development of Side Channel Attack-resistant programs. This research is an extension of existing work on protected processors, which have been used in memory protection; our contribution is to explore whether similar architectures can be used for Side Channel Attack protection. This research is related to homomorphic encryption, which has been used in secure evaluation; our difference, however, lies in our focus on a processor architecture that incorporates protection mechanisms to enable the development of Side Channel Attack-resistant programs. This research is an essential step toward realizing program obfuscation and contributing to the field of software protection. Ultimately, we hope that our design will spur the development of side-channel attack-resistant programs, thereby promoting the development of more trustworthy software. This research is an important effort to realize software protection, and we hope that our design, the Virtual Protected Framework, will serve as a useful reference for software developers and the community at large. Recent breakthroughs in language modeling have enabled analyses of text data
without needing annotated labels, which has become a highly valued skill.
Two key areas representing unsupervised and few-shot analysis capabilities from
language models are (i) assessing semantic meaning changes when words are
replaced and (ii) predicting text based on incomplete or missing information.
However, existing methods often test these capabilities in isolation, limiting
our understanding of their individual strengths and weaknesses. To address this,
we introduce a unified framework for evaluating these tasks by using
pretrained language models effectively. Our method allows for the exploration of
various training and inference strategies across multiple benchmarks, including
unsupervised and few-shot settings. We also provide new insights into the
relative efficacy of baseline methods involving language models and highlight
potential areas for improvement in these techniques. The unified framework and
associated code are now available for reproduction of our results. Keywords:
Language-models, Unsupervised, Few-shot, Semantics, Infilling.

High-definition hyperspectral images, featuring multiple color dimensions in each pixel, offer enhanced visual information. This research leverages these images in weakly-supervised semantic segmentation tasks. Specifically, we enhance hyperspectral pixels into effective image classifiers, capitalizing on the inherent color meaning. This approach enables the creation of meaningful image segments using simple, low-level image characteristics. To facilitate effective image segmentation, we introduce an unsupervised hyperspectral image transformation technique, leveraging established color meaning associations. The resulting image segments, produced by an unsupervised classifier, serve as high-level semantic categories. To connect these categories with image features, we utilize an established weakly-supervised semantic segmentation solution, adapting it for hyperspectral images. The integration of hyperspectral information with traditional image features yields an aggregate set of image descriptors. Finally, we employ these descriptors in a weakly-supervised semantic segmentation task, capitalizing on the extended information. The results demonstrate that the proposed method, designed for Cityscape dataset, outperforms alternative approaches, including pure color-based method, domain adaptation, and image transformation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chen-546/HyperspectralSeg.

To facilitate effective session-based suggestion, users need relevant information presented at the right time. However, suggestions provided by a recommendation model are often influenced by its inherent biases, leading to the presentation of less relevant data earlier in the session. This problem can be addressed through a framework that utilizes user feedback and existing knowledge to guide the recommendation model and direct the presentation of suggestions. Given that user feedback is scarce and largely negative, a co-training method is employed to leverage both unstructured session data and structured knowledge to improve the quality of the recommendation model. This co-training approach is further enhanced using a self-guided technique to prevent the model from relying too heavily on existing knowledge, thus optimizing the presentation of suggestions throughout the session. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated the success of this proposed method over a range of baselines and a deep learning-based graph-based co-training approach. Specifically, it has been shown that the proposed method achieves a 0.234% gain in click-through rate and a 0.235% gain in net user benefit in suggestion quality. Additionally, it has been found that the self-guided technique accounts for 70% of the improvement in click-through rate achieved by the session-guided co-training method. Code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/yangyangyang/SGGC. Experimental data can be accessed through https://data.world/datalab/sbs. In this paper, we explore the differential structures of various complexes of graphs, deriving an explicit rule for the exterior product of differential forms. We identify a key property, invariant under the graph renaming operation, which governs the differential structure of these complexes. We apply this understanding to derive an explicit formula for the exterior product of differential forms in the Feynman integral complex, resulting in a novel integration formula. Moreover, we leverage this integration formula to derive a general expression for the primitive part of a Feynman integral. It's noteworthy that our method for graph renaming relies on recent results from combinatorial topology, specifically the concept of 2-division of a graph, allowing our findings to be applicable to graphs having multiple loop edges and a single vertex. Lastly, we converge on the differential structure of the space of weighted graphs equipped with a distinguished set of loop edges, achieving our conclusion through a nontrivial generalization of established results from differential geometry. We expect our findings to be instrumental in future research into the cohomology and physics of Feynman integrals. We also include a detailed appendix that provides a concise overview of the relevant concepts from the 2-division of graphs. We hope this will be a valuable resource for early-stage researchers and serve as a useful reference for the broader theoretical physics community. Additionally, the associated supplementary material includes a comprehensive collection of published and unpublished works, totaling 25 references, that provide a thorough foundation for the central concepts and results discussed in this paper. These include the cohomology of Feynman integrals, graph complexes, and 2-division of graphs, as well as their far-reaching connections to the study of the cohomology of the moduli spaces of smooth closed manifolds. We eagerly invite readers to peruse this supplementary material in full. We have taken great care to ensure that our work is disseminated in a transparent and accessible manner, and we hope that our findings will prove valuable in the ongoing pursuit of new insights in the field. In a liquid intelligence framework, recurrent neural networks can mimic biological brain function by dynamically processing sequential data. This study explores the role of category-specific object attributes in guiding information flow within a liquid recurrent neural network designed for object classification. We examine the sensitivity of its internal representations to selective manipulations of different visual attributes in line with those typically encountered in the natural world (e.g., shapes within sizes) versus those that are less prevalent (e.g., sizes within shapes). We find that the first type of manipulation strongly influences internal representations and thus object classifications, whereas the second type has a minimal impact. This points to the possibility that efficient object classifications are facilitated by leveraging established, category-specific associations between objects and their attributes. Once such knowledge is incorporated into the network, it may focus on refining and consolidating this information through ongoing learning. This study provides a novel, computationally informed understanding of object representation and attribute interactions within a artificial neural system. Additionally, it offers a theoretical basis for the design of novel artificial intelligence architectures that could potentially ground object representations in real-world category-specific attribute structures. This could, in turn, enhance the overall efficiency of these systems. We suggest exploring similar approaches in biological neural systems to deepen their interpretation. This study is comprised of a series of experiments that progressively investigate the effect of different visual attribute manipulations on object classifications within a liquid recurrent neural network. We find that the best-performing model is one in which the internal representations of the network are most sensitive to manipulations of attribute categories rather than individual objects. This sensitivity is strongly reflected in its internal representations and is consistent across multiple scenarios featuring distinct attribute categories. This study is the first to examine the role of category-specific attribute structures in guiding information flow within artificial neural systems and their internal representations. It identifies a crucial distinction between two types of visual attribute manipulations: those that are typical (e.g., shapes within sizes) versus those that are less prevalent (e.g., sizes within shapes). This distinction has far-reaching implications for the design and interpretation of neural networks, particularly those trained for object classification tasks. We suggest extending the liquid recurrent neural networks used in this study to their analog counterparts within biological brains, which could provide a novel understanding of object representation and attribute interactions. In one-dimensional systems with correlated electrons, we investigate the effect of interactions on the topological characteristics inherent to the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model, which feature a non-Hermitian band structure. The correlations, born out of the electron-electon interaction, cause lattice deformation and ultimately lead to a reduction in the topological rank of the system. Specifically, the correlations abolish the chiral symmetry present in the SSH model, thereby eliminating the extra topological characteristic. The reduction in topological rank is demonstrated through the defined topological characteristics after the interaction. Moreover, under specific conditions, the correlations can induce a topological transition from a trivial to a non-Hermitian insulator. Our study paves the way for the understanding of the correlation-induced reduction of topological rank in one-dimensional systems with non-Hermitian topological characteristics. The underlying mathematical tools employed in this research can also be applied to the study of other topological systems. The results can be replicated using quantum Monte Carlo numerical methods, and the code used for this purpose is available upon request. Several techniques have been proposed recently to tackle optimization problems with uncertain quantities or constraints, and numerous methods have been developed to tackle these issues effectively. Although some of these techniques have shown impressive performance, they often lack readily available code bases, forcing researchers to invest significant time in implementing them from scratch. To address this challenge, we introduce an open-source platform called LibOPT, designed to facilitate the rapid development of novel soft optimization methods by building upon existing ones. Featuring a modular structure and extensive collection of over 300 tested functions, LibOPT enables seamless extension of existing algorithms or comparison of multiple techniques to solve specific problems, thereby saving researchers a significant amount of time, approximately 70-85, as demonstrated through real-world examples. In quantum theory, particles exhibit duality, with the same particle displaying both wave-like and particle-like behaviors. Nonrelativistic quantum mechanics describes particles using a specific function in a specific space, and the identity of a particle is defined by this function. However, in theories deviating from standard space (such as noncommutative geometry and deformed special relativity), the building blocks of matter may not fit the standard particle description, potentially altering their identity. We investigate the modification of quantum objects in nonstandard space and time, revealing ambiguities in their composition and showing that any object can be any other object in such frameworks. As a result, we have no definitive description of the building blocks of matter in these spaces. While this uncertainty may be mitigated by further measurements, it also presents an opportunity for more general approaches to quantum matter that are consistent across different geometric frameworks. We conclude by highlighting the potential for more universal quantum matter descriptions and initiating a debate on the nature of quantum objects in nonstandard space. To advance this discussion, we open a query list, and we invite fellow experts to contribute. We will later compile these contributions and open a second round of discussion. Please note that this text is a summary of the debate's initial phase, and it will be expanded with contributions from other experts in a subsequent response. We apply the two-photon absorption transient current technique to study
properties of wide bandgap semiconductors. We utilize two coherent laser beams
with overlapping spots to transmit energy into single-crystalline diamond.
By varying the laser polarization's angle, we generate an anisotropic current
signal related to the crystal's charge transport direction, allowing for a
three-dimensional (3D) mapping of the material's charge transport properties in
a 2D pattern. Our findings reveal charge transport variations in (100) and
(111) diamond surfaces. The ratio of the transport coefficients $\gamma$,
calculated from the light, directly correlates with the crystal's charge
transport direction, thus providing unique 3D charge transport maps. These
maps cannot be obtained with traditional optical methods that measure the
transverse and longitudinal components separately. Moreover, our study
investigates the role of charge carrier generation in the bulk and the
interface in determining the charge transport properties, revealing that
different mechanisms produce distinct 3D transport patterns. These studies
will greatly benefit the development of single-crystalline diamond quantum
information systems by identifying a relationship between the crystal's
charge transport properties and its unique 3D structure. Lastly, our work's
findings are applicable not only to diamond but also to other wide bandgap
semiconductors.

Social media platforms are facing significant concerns regarding the spread of derogatory and offensive content, particularly gender-based hate speech. This type of language not only causes emotional distress to individuals targeted, but also contributes to a more severe problem - the perpetuation of gender prejudice in society. In light of this issue, researchers have begun to focus on the analysis and classification of hate speech, with Arabic being a key target. This study contributes to the field by introducing an innovative approach to detecting misogynous content in Arabic social media. The proposed framework is an improvement over existing ones as it is more efficient, empowering Arab women in the digital space. This work is the first to explore the application of a specific deep learning model, combining the powers of BiLSTM, Co-Attention, and Feature-Interaction Layers. Experiments were conducted on two distinct datasets, yielding promising results and providing valuable insights that can guide future studies in this domain. This research is expected to enhance the capabilities of machine learning models in detecting hate speech and open up new avenues for exploring other complex social media phenomena in Arabic. This research also contributes to the accelerated training of deep learning models for NLP tasks, a concept the principal investigator introduced in 2020. The findings of this study have practical implications and can be directly utilized in real-world applications, including social media filtering systems and Arabic text classification services. The code for this research has been made publicly available for the benefit of the scientific community. Keywords: Arabic, misogyney, deep learning, NLP, text classification, misogyny detection, social media, misogyny classification.

The process of summarizing one or multiple documents involves condensing their content into a more compact yet equivalent format, typically half to two-thirds the original size, to facilitate easier understanding and comprehension. There are two primary approaches to text summarization: inductive and selective methods. The inductive method directly produces summaries, while selective methods identify and extract key components from the original content. This study focuses on a constructive, extractive methodology involving the creation of a graph to represent sentences as nodes and their importance as weights, enabling the selection of vital information through graph theory and color coding techniques. We examined two color coding methods: the first relies on the dominance of sentences by other components, and the other assesses sentence importance using both local and global criteria. We tested two sentence ranking strategies: the first relies on the similarity between sentences, and the other considers both similarity and key component associations. We analyzed four key component types: naming entities, parts-of-speech, sentence length, and coherence with the document's overall structure. We employed two similarity measures: the shared naming entities and the edited similarity shape. We conducted exhaustive searches for the optimal coloring configuration and compared the results with the approach of starting with the optimal coloring configuration after analyzing the dominance of each sentence. We performed experiments using the standard dataset consisting of 50 abstracts and applied the traditional evaluation metrics: N, P, and F1. We also analyzed the sum of the weights of the selected sentences and the length of the chosen sentences. We utilized the t-test and chi-squared tests to compare the results and found that the proposed methodology outperforms the approach of starting with the optimal coloring configuration after analyzing the dominance of each sentence, achieving a higher F1 score of 0.879 against 0.823, respectively. Additionally, we found no statistically significant difference between the two methods in the selected sentences' weights and their distribution. This paper presents an algorithm inspired by the signature-driven shape interpretation approach from computer-aided design, but adapted for solving polynomial system solving tasks. The algebraic framework equivalent to the shape interpretation method is known as the Shapiro shape interpretation method. This adaptation specifically addresses the task of determining the Locus with non-trivial topology resulting from a particular parameter or set of parameters taking on specific values in a parameter space. The proposed algorithm is a part of the PyLocus software package that is also discussed in this article, focusing on evaluating the Locus with respect to one parameter. The PyLocus toolbox is built on top of SageMath and SageMath is used to describe the underlying algebraic structure, while the algorithm itself is described using a combination of algebraic and dynamic formal languages. This new algorithm is designed to be compatible with existing solving methods already implemented in computer algebra systems, such as SageMath, for evaluating polynomial systems at specific points or sets of points. The algorithm is a signature-driven interpretation method that uses a signature consisting of pairs of polynomials from the given polynomial system and a parameter value, with which it computes a topological space as a quotient space, equivalent to the Locus with non-trivial topology resulting from those parameter values. The algorithm then proceeds to present a representation of the resulting topological space, typically as a union of algebraically defined spheres, providing their respective radii and centers, in addition to any points not lying within any sphere in the union. The algorithm further describes how to present these spherical components as disjoint unions of algebraically defined balls and their respective radii and centers, effectively presenting the topological space as a discrete structure consisting of these parameter-dependent algebraic sets, their associated radii and centers. A longstanding problem posed by Szele in 1943, later reinvented by Turan, seeks to find the minimum number of vertices needed for a d-dimensional convex body, assuming it contains at least r convex faces.  In 2013, Patai and Szabo essentially settled the problem, answering a question first posed by Erdos about the minimal number of faces in a d-dimensional convex body containing n vertices.  By doing so, they almost solved Turan's problem, determining that any d-dimensional convex body, regardless of its number of vertices, must have at least $2r-1$ vertices if it is not a tetrahedron.  In our research, we almost settle the entire problem by deriving a lower bound for the number of vertices in any d-dimensional convex body, regardless of its number of faces, if it is not a tetrahedron.  To do this, we count the number of its bivalent vertices, discovering that this amount is sufficient to construct $r$ convex faces, assuming a certain structure for the body's boundary.  In many cases, this lower bound is optimal.  In others, such as when d is 1 or 2 but not 3, we prove it to be almost optimal.  In our research, we use three fundamental theorems about convex bodies, as well as three new lemmas, to derive these results.  In particular, we generalize the Borsuk's Theorem, previously applied to convex bodies by Patai and Szabo, and also applied to polytopes by Imre, to any d-dimensional convex body. Achieving visually appealing results when representing line junctions on vector maps is a complex task. Typically, maps use a pixel-based anti-aliasing technique that involves calculating the area of each junction with a specified radius. However, this method is insufficient for rendering line junctions due to the significant number of pixels involved, leading to distorted junction shapes on high-density pixel screens and inaccurate rendering of text or icon overlays on top of line maps. This issue can be resolved through the implementation of a spatial anti-aliasing technique that considers the individual pixels of a pixel circle. However, this method is also insufficient, as it fails to take into account the screen resolution and font quality of the target system. This problem can be overcome through the integration of a spatial anti-aliasing technique that incorporates the screen resolution and font quality. However, this would require a substantial amount of computation, notably by multiplying the radius of each junction by the screen resolution and font quality, which is impractical for real-time rendering on mobile devices. This problem can be resolved through the integration of a practical and efficient spatial anti-aliasing technique that balances visual quality and performance. Specifically, this can be achieved by modifying the anti-aliasing radius based on the screen resolution and font quality without multiplying it, while ensuring a smooth and high-quality visual experience. This approach involves combining the principles of a circular area anti-aliasing technique and a spatial anti-aliassing technique that considers the individual pixels of a circular area, while effectively eliminating unnecessary computations and optimizing performance for mobile devices. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach, when compared against a range of existing anti-aliasing methods, yields a line junction shape accuracy within 1 pixel, while also ensuring a frame rate of at least 10fps on high-density pixel screens and accurately rendering text or icon overlays on top of line maps. Additionally, this approach is also compatible with GPU acceleration for enhanced performance on mobile devices.
