Incident analysis is a vital component of power system research, however, analyzing incidents in the distribution segment is hindered by a lack of standardized data. The costs associated with deploying sophisticated monitoring equipment across an extensive distribution network are prohibitive, thereby limiting access to reliable data. As a result, existing studies rely on anecdotal experience, thereby distilling valuable insights into rule-based methods that can learn from experience. This paper introduces a novel data-driven approach rooted in experience that enables identification of incidents within distribution networks, an approach that can be adapted to accommodate areas with limited incident data. The proposed method's efficacy was tested using the standard 12-kV model distribution feeders from the IEEE. The results show that incident patterns can be accurately learned even when data coverage is less than 20%. The approach was further validated on a real-world sub-network within the primary distribution sector of an Israeli city. The findings reveal that this approach can function effectively even when data is scarce and can still enable substantial improvements in incident recognition. We provide a comprehensive description of quadrics within the context of categorical geometry by establishing a one-to-one relationship between certain categories and quadrics in projective spaces. Specifically, our results relate the category of finite-dimensional hermitian forms over a commutative ring to the quadrics in a projective space constructed using that ring's bilinear forms. This categorification offers an abstract representation of quadrics, which enables the study of morphism spaces between quadrics through the use of category theory. Moreover, it enables the development of a homological algebra for quadrics and facilitates the investigation of fibre products and other universal constructs in this context. The evidence for our claims consists of a series of detailed diagrams illustrating the categories and quadrics involved. Ultimately, this framework is poised to provide a suitable ground for generalising quadrics to arbitrary algebraic geometries. Our approach is inspired by the established theories of projective algebra and projective trigonometry. As such, the proposed generalisation should be compatible with these existing theories. Furthermore, this framework is anticipated to be closely linked with the category of hermitian forms, which is a key component of k-theory. Specifically, it is expected to play a pivotal role in the pending proof of the k-theoretic generalisation of the euler-poincare formula for arithmetic quadrics. Additionally, this framework is anticipated to be a crucial component in the ongoing development of a projective description of motives. The proposed categorification of quadrics should also serve as a prototype for generalising arbitrary algebraic geometric objects and, ultimately, for extending this process to topological and noncommutative quadrics. Lastly, this framework is expected to provide fresh insights into the classical quadrics that have already been studied for so long. Specifically, it is anticipated that category theory will shed a new and interesting light on the projective algebra, projective linear algebra and projective trigonometry that have been explored in such great detail. Text games, used for natural language processing research, typically have limitations on player input, game advancement, and data collection. To overcome these constraints, we have developed TextWorldExpress, a new framework that combines multiple text games into a single, larger game. This combines the advantages of various games while bypassing their individual limitations. By allowing players to control multiple games at once, TextWorldExpress increases game step counts from a previous high of around 3,000 to over one million. This enables the creation of substantially larger datasets. Our system was tested in a scenario where it learned to follow a map by navigating through several text games, all while its human players had to guess the map representation. This experiment not only broke the previous record for game step counts, but also showed improvements in both game agent performance and human intuition. Our research resulted in the creation of the TextWorldExpress dataset, which contains over 370,000 game steps and shows improved results compared to baseline models. This dataset can be accessed via a web interface for performing competitive evaluations. Additionally, the code for TextWorldExpress has been released under an open-source license. It includes tools for both the text games we used in our study and the system we developed for overcoming the usual limitations. Our hope is that TextWorldExpress will become a valuable resource for the natural language processing research community. It has the potential to significantly expand the scale of text game-based research while also facilitating the comparison of different approaches. Furthermore, TextWorldExpress can serve as a general framework for tackling various problems by imitating multiple issues at once. We believe this could be a valuable asset to the research community due to its potential for addressing a wide range of challenging problems. TextWorldExpress, in particular, demonstrated more robust and versatile performance compared to baseline models in our study. It successfully identified the layout of a map through game step counts that were 250-300 times greater than those achieved by the best performing individual game agents. Our human subjects, in contrast, were only able to accurately guess the map representation after about 1,600 game steps. This marked the point at which TextWorldExpress surpassed their performance. Inspired by Deligne's work, we establish that there are only finitely many algebraic functions, including non-constant ones, defined over a specific domain and satisfy certain conditions. This applies to both low-degree polynomials and rational functions. The proof relies on several key concepts including arithmetic on algebraic curves, Faltings' theorem, and a theorem by Nogin, which together provide the necessary tools for modeling algebraic functions, bounding their complexity, and ultimately proving the finiteness of the functions in question. Additionally, we provide several examples that illustrate the non-triviality of the functions we are considering. Finally, we make a conjecture about the finiteness of linear functions, which we believe to be true, and explain why it would have significant implications if proven. A key operational requirement for successful human-robot collaboration is easily grasping the underlying physics of the task at hand. However, the operational dynamics of a task are often deeply rooted in the environment in which the task is executed and consequently vary significantly between disparate domains. In our research, we address the novel challenge of adapting a learning framework that is based on observations from a training domain to a different operational domain, all while accounting for variations in both the identity of the robot and the shape of the environment. To achieve this, we develop a specialized alignment technique that takes into consideration the curved nature of the operational manifold and utilizes optimized normal vectors to facilitate smooth domain adaptation. Through experimental validation, we demonstrate that our proposed approach facilitates seamless adaptation of the learning framework to new domains with little to no additional training, thereby extending the usefulness of the training. Additionally, we observed that our approach is highly resilient to distortions in the shape of the training environment. The findings of this study open up new avenues for employing learning frameworks in complex collaborative tasks that involve humans and robots working together. Deep learning models, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are widely used for classification tasks due to their robust performance. However, standard CNNs may not fully utilize the spatial information in images. To address this issue, a new model called Orientation Convolutive Networks (OCNs) is proposed. In OCNs, the conventional convolutional operators are replaced with the orientation convolutive operators, which incorporate the properties of the Zernike polynomials. This replacement enables the network to directly learn and incorporate valuable spatial information. Experimental results on four publicly available databases indicate that the proposed OCNs outperform the conventional CNNs. A significant improvement in accuracy was observed on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 databases, and the results show that the parameters of OCNs are 1.07 to 3.64 times those of CNNs, which is an acceptable cost for the potential performance gains. Additionally, the proposed OCNs were compared with other advanced architectures, demonstrating their superiority. Furthermore, the implemented experiments on the Tiny ImageNet dataset yield a 0.4072 mAP evaluation result for the classification task. To validate the importance of spatial information, numerous ablation studies were performed using the ResNet-18 model. The results indicate that the parameter count of the modified model is 1.08 to 2.48 times that of the baseline CNN, in exchange for a potential performance boost of 0.76 and 1.34 percent in terms of top-1 accuracy, for the two datasets respectively. A public PyTorch implementation of the proposed model is available for other researchers to utilize. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that the proposed Orientation Convolutive Networks represent a significant advancement in the field and may serve as a useful model for other researchers to use as a baseline in future studies. Additionally, the associated source code can be found at: https://github.com/fataldev/Orientation_Convolutive_Networks. The success of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) depends significantly on their underlying graph structure. In the context of point cloud processing, several methods have attempted to utilize GCNs by designing networks based on Euclidean distance or local neighborhood, that is, k-NN graph. However, these approaches fall short in global point cloud processing due to their narrow scope. This work aims to broaden the k-NN graph's influence, effectively extending its support. By doing so, GCN filters are allowed to absorb the underlying graph's effects, thereby increasing the network's expressiveness. To accomplish this, we propose a simple yet effective strategy that modulates the strength of GCN filters based on the relative proximity of nodes in the k-NN graph, thereby simulating a semi-definite Gaussian kernel. By increasing the network's depth, we demonstrate the equivalence of our model to a neighboring node based on the Chebyshev polynomial approximation. Furthermore, we present a novel network that is capable of global point cloud processing, along with extensive experiments that validate its effectiveness. Nevertheless, key information about potential Earth-like planets remains elusive: what are the chemical compositions of these worlds? In this study, we draw on data from the HARPS-N transit spectrum of K2-22b, a Saturn-sized gas giant orbiting an active M-dwarf star. By analyzing abundance patterns of gases within the atmosphere of K2-22b, we infer the type of processes that created its parent star's metallic elements. This analysis also sheds light on the composition of the star's convective envelope, its outer boundary layer, and the cores of rocky planets, guided by hydrostatic and photoelectric models. The resulting findings suggest that the star's convective zone contains approximately 1-2% metal by mass, a percentage consistent with observations of the star's spectral features. This value is lower than that previously estimated for the Sun, often used as a base standard in planetary science. The most reliable rock formation models indicate that planets formed in this system contain less iron and more silicate minerals than those in our Solar System, shaped by the unique stellar winds and radiative pressure exerted on the star. This study's findings contribute to our understanding of terrestrial planets' compositions, their formation processes, and the potential for life on planets in this system, all factors influenced by the star's distinct metal enrichment. The resulting planetary bodies may resemble those in habitable zones around low-mass stars, such as those in the Tres Colinas system or those with metal-poor compositions. The unique chemical compositions of these planets may stem from their formation in distinct stellar environments. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Notwithstanding, the effectiveness of CSI is constrained by its dynamic and spatially scattered nature. Consequently, features extracted by the DNN may be suboptimal and prone to bias. To address this limitation, this study presents an alternative approach that combines attention mechanisms with CSI, to selectively emphasize IMs with significant geometric implications, thereby improving feature relevance. To this end, a channel attention module (CAM) and a spatial attention module (SAM) have been devised to respectively focus on the time domain and the cross-beam domain, thereby refining feature extraction. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the system's capability to achieve localizing performance on par with or superior to outcomes obtained through CSI feature aggregation (CFAG) and conventional DNNs. Moreover, the trained networks can achieve impressive accuracy when subjected to stringent testing conditions, comprising significant channel interference and camera malfunction simulations. To verify the proposed solution's efficiency, a proof-of-concept prototype utilizing an Raspberry Pi was developed for experimental validation. The presented work is expected to benefit researchers working on wireless localization, particularly those utilizing CSI-based approaches. This paper launches a comprehensive investigation into modal logic, with a specific focus on the three most widely studied types: epistemic, temporal, and doxastic logic. Unlike existing research that typically focuses on specific logics, this paper aims to delve into the underlying mathematical structures of these logics, with the ultimate goal of establishing a unified framework for modal logic. In addition to the familiar epistemic, temporal, and doxastic logic, this paper also considers more recent developments in the field, including the modal logics of ability, and applies the mathematical structures of modal logic to study both traditional and advanced modal logic. The study begins by examining the topological structures of three basic modal logics and progresses to the more advanced modal logic of ability, using the topological structure known as $C$-space. This paper represents a starting point for a broader research initiative that aims to provide a unified mathematical approach to modal logic. The project's website at https://unimodallogic.github.io/ provides further details. The associated software package can be downloaded from https://github.com/unimodallogic/unimodallogic. Achieving accuracy in scientific predictions is crucial, yet uncertainties inevitably accompany these predictions. Ambiguity around uncertainty estimates, however, hinders the comparison of different quantitative methods. The present paper evaluates, differentiates, and assesses various techniques for quantifying uncertainty that can be used in scientific machine learning. Initially, the paper outlines the objectives of uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning. Next, the paper categorizes techniques into two groups: those that generate multiple predictive distributions through sampling or approximation, and those that determine uncertainty metrics through optimization. The paper then examines techniques of the first category, focusing on latent variable models, ensemble learning, and adversarial methods, as well as uncertainty metrics of the second category, focusing on empirical uncertainty estimation. The paper then evaluates these techniques using benchmark tests and an actual scientific problem: predicting the output of photochemical reactions based on their input. The paper seeks to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of uncertainty quantification in scientific machine learning and aims to contribute to future research in this area. The code used in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/finan-project/ambiguation. In the future, the paper's findings will be expanded to encompass various applications in scientific machine learning. The paper will eventually be submitted for review to a scholarly journal. When solving large-scale Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), the value function approximation typically employs a neural network as an approximation tool. By iterating on the Generalized Minimum Residual Method (GMRES), the approximate solution can be converged within a specified tolerance. However, the computational cost of GMRES iteration is high. By breaking the iteration into two loops, a modified algorithm is proposed, allowing for the exchange of two matrices at the beginning. Utilizing a preconditioner and specifying a tolerance for each loop, the approximate solution can be obtained within two iterations. This modification is equivalent to performing GMRES for only two iterations and has the benefit of reducing the computational cost without sacrificing accuracy. Moreover, when equipped with the ability to regulate the precision of the approximate solution, the algorithm can provide a range of solutions between exact and approximate options. An experimental demonstration shows the performance of the modified algorithm compared to the standard GMRES iteration. Additionally, the algorithms' potential applications are discussed in relation to other interior point methods (IPMs) that converge monotonically to the optimal solution. Due to not converging monotonically in general, a criterion is proposed to determine whether the approximate solution is close enough to the optimal solution. As such, this algorithm can provide solutions that are either superior or adequate to the optimal option. When equipped with the capacity to regulate the precision of the approximate solution, the algorithm can also provide a range of solutions between the optimal and approximate options. An examination through experimentation shows the potential of this modified algorithm. The source code for the algorithm is available at https://github.com/charleselph/imprecise_gmres_strategical_iteration. Two examples are provided at https://github.com/charleselph/mdps_approximation_testbed to compare the performance of the modified algorithm with standard GMRES iteration. An earlier version of this work was presented at the 2022 NeurIPS Workshop on Deeper Renewal of Machine Learning and Optimization. Additionally, the related article titled 'Inferential GMRES: Convergence of Generalized Minimum Residual Methods in Markov Decision Processes' has been published in Mathematics, Volume 10, Issue 10, pages 1838-1851, 2022. We investigate an inverse problem where a simulation's operation is reversed to meet a specific timeline, presenting a challenging non-linear issue. Due to the high computational costs of simulation models, solving the inverse problem quantitatively proves impractical. We propose tackling this problem through a non-parametric, multi-dimensional approach called multi-dimensional multiple contour estimation which can efficiently handle complex, dependent variables like time series data. We compare the performance of various methods such as kernel regression, k-nearest neighbors, support vector machines, and random forest within a simulation framework for evaluating the performance of wind turbine technology. The proposed approach offers an accurate and practical solution to these high-computation, time-sensitive simulation models, providing a meaningful outcome in a feasible timeframe. Moreover, this method facilitates the computation of related statistical measures, thus providing a more comprehensive insight into these simulation models. We illustrate the performance of this approach using a well-known simulation framework for evaluating the performance of wind turbine technology called BEMWOW. This article includes detailed information on reproducing the results. The proposed method has been published in a separate article. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals the interplay between network structure and disease dynamics. However, as the disease model becomes more complex, so does the required network topology for the avoidance of epidemics. In two dimensions, this topological criterion is essentially the planar nature of the network, allowing for the application of mathematical techniques, like complex analysis, to analyze the problem. Nevertheless, as we explore more complex network topologies, such as hypergraphs, the ability to use similar mathematical approaches fails, and a different methodology is needed to solve the problem. By employing an entirely new method based on the weakly Riemannian structure and the $\bar{\partial}$-operator, we are able to derive a spectral condition for the non-existence of epidemics in hypergraphs and establish a general theorem for this scenario. As a direct application of our spectral approach, we are able to determine the critical threshold for the survival of an immunized population within a hypergraph structure. Ultimately, this research seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for the extinction vs. survival analysis of epidemics within various network topologies, starting with hypergraphs as a pioneering case. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm to find the non-existence spectrum of an epidemic on a given hypergraph. Furthermore, we derive an approximation formula for the edge and net out-degrees distributions in hypergraphs. By analyzing the distribution of out-degrees in a hypergraph, and comparing it to that of a corresponding complete graph, which corresponds to a model for epidemics, we find that the difference in their spectral behavior leads to an inequality that could be useful in analyzing the behavior of epidemics on hypergraphs. This research also introduces ratio theorems for the spectrum of an epidemic on a hypergraph, analogous to similar theorems for the spectrum of a graph, and concludes by introducing numerous problems for further investigation. Finally, we illustrate our theoretical findings with the help of numerous numerical examples. Developing a practical and effective object recognition system is relatively easy
when working with a single visual input, but achieving this in a multimodal setting
(that includes multiple sensory inputs) is more complicated due to the diverse nature
of these inputs and the challenge of integrating them effectively into a unified representation.
Although some recent multimodal neural network designs have achieved significant performance
gains, many of these solutions are specific to particular modalities and cannot be adapted
easily to other types of sensory input. Furthermore, many traditional multimodal neural
networks rely on complicated designs that are difficult to implement in practice.
This study presents a new and versatile multimodal neural network called the K-fan
Multimodal Neural Network, which is capable of handling multiple types of sensory input
and is easily adaptable to different configurations to suit a wide range of applications.
Our work is driven by two key observations: first, not all sensory inputs are equally
valuable for a particular task, and building a system that can selectively filter these
inputs can help to simplify design and improve performance; second, different sensory inputs
can often be represented effectively using a common set of underlying concepts, and
building a system that is capable of identifying these core ideas can help to enable
inter-modal communication and facilitate more efficient learning.
Our K-fan multimodal neural network is designed to tackle these challenges by incorporating
two key components: the "K-fan" filter, which allows it to selectively process and integrate
information from different sensory inputs based on their relative values to the target
outcome; and a shared-representation architecture that enables it to identify underlying
concepts that can bridge different modalities and facilitate inter-modal communication.
When tested on a range of object recognition tasks, our system performed remarkably well
in comparison to other leading solutions, and we provide extensive analysis to explain its
success and to suggest ways in which it could be further developed in the future. Our code

Declarative parallel programming is gaining traction due to its natural parallelism, 
where specifications are written in logical form and the parallelism is implied 
automatically. However, verifying the correctness of multithreaded programs written 
in this paradigm is a challenging task. Traditional state exploration tools are not 
well-suited for declarative programs because of their reliance on imperative 
modelling techniques that introduce unnecessary serialisation points, limiting the 
program's parallelism. In contrast, this work presents McMini, a configurable DPOR- 
based model checker specifically designed for declarative parallel programs. It 
employs a novel combination of McMillan's sequence of steps and the structural 
composition of declarative programs, offering an automatic parallel verification 
procedure. Furthermore, McMini's algorithm is parametrised by a new concept called 
"parallelisation scope", allowing developers to fine-tune the programme's 
parallel structure and improve verification efficiency. In the paper's experimental 
evaluation, McMini outperforms a previously established state exploration tool, 
yielding up to a 7 times faster verification time and up to a 7 times smaller search 
space for a range of complex programmes. The McMini tool is available at https://mcmini.github.io.

Spoofing counter-measures (SCs) are an integral part of securing voice-based security systems, ensuring that only genuine speech is admitted. A leading method among SCs involves using differential entropy-based features (DEFs) as an activation function in a neural network. However, this approach has drawbacks, such as decreased robustness against sophisticated attacks and a limited capacity for distinguishing between attack types. To address these issues, we introduce an improved SC system that utilizes an enhanced vigilance-based activation function (VAAF) built upon AUTOENCODER (AE) networks. This VAAF activation function surpasses prior methods in vigilance, distinguishing between speech types and resisting spoofing attempts more effectively. To optimize our approach, we incorporate three criteria: classification accuracy for spoofing, classification accuracy for non-spoofing, and difference in accuracy for spoofing and non-spoofing. This strategic selection enables our system to distinguish between genuine and spoofed speech with elevated vigilance and improved recognition performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VAAF-based SC system yields: (a) improved anti-spoofing performance across various attack types; (b) augmented vigilance in recognizing various attack types; (c) a simplified decision process with a single parameter for any type of attack; and (d) superior performance compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. To validate our approach, we utilized the ASVspoof 2019 benchmark in the baseline scenario. Our approach is now made available online with the following codes: https://github.com/hjzhihwan/VigilanceVF.git. Additionally, the corresponding datasets and short-lived desktop versions can be accessed via: https://hjzhihwan.github.io/VSVF/. polarization can be broken down into components related to the angular
momentum of the photon pair and their mutual influence. Its characteristics
depend on the angle at the source of the photons and their state when measured. 
A situation where the sunlight is partially linearly polarized offers an
opportunity to observe this asymmetry in practice, potentially leading to a
new method for detecting circular polarization in natural sources. Moreover, 
this asymmetry may serve as a indicator of macrorealism or local hidden
variables in nature. Finally, this asymmetry could also be studied using
linearly polarized photon pairs by incorporating a muon decay as the source.

A new method to evaluate the characteristics of planar microwave devices at the nanoscale is developed by utilizing a terahertz snare-and-share technique. This technique, based on a conventional microwave setup, allows for identifying changes in the local terahertz conductivity of a device. This is possible by comparing the properties of and, ultimately, the electromagnetic fields produced by a test sample and a reference substrate when exposed to terahertz radiation. This method is used to analyze the local terahertz conductivity of an LCR circuit and reveal variations in terahertz field patterns. Such analysis could lead to a better comprehension of device functionality and potentially enable the development of more advanced nanoscale electronics. It is further demonstrated that the same setup can be adapted for optical nanoscopy by replacing terahertz radiation with near-infrared light, thereby making it possible to study the near-infrared properties of devices. This could potentially facilitate the development of a terahertz version of optical nanoscopy.

This study aims to address a concern that novel investment methods might draw resources away from established strategies, causing them to underperform. To explore this issue, the researchers employ an agent-based model, simulating a population of long-term, risk-averse investors who can opt for two types of novel and traditional investment tactics. As a novel tactic emerges, initially lacking history, the investigation includes three scenarios with varying levels of information availability. The results indicate that novel tactics do not necessarily compromise existing strategies. Moreover, the impact of an emerging tactic on existing ones depends on several factors, including its past performance compared to traditional methods. When novel tactics are relatively unsuccessful, they do not negatively affect traditional strategies. However, when they outperform existing options, they redirect resources towards their own type, but this does not harm traditional strategies. Ultimately, the most successful tactic emerges as the dominant choice, outperforming others. Based on these findings, the risk associated with embracing an emerging investment approach appears to be minimal. It is only when an emerging tactic significantly underperforms, replicating the historical data of an existing strategy, that it might inadvertently harm traditional investors. Researchers identified a significant flaw in network security monitoring systems, specifically those using protocol identification for flow analysis. This weakness, which affects over 70% of such systems,, can be exploited by an attacker to confuse the security monitoring system into misidentifying network traffic. By causing the system to mistake one protocol for another, the attacker gains valuable insight into the target network, including previously inaccessible information. Due to the relatively simple methods involved in exploiting this flaw, researchers believe it poses a substantial threat to network security. Notably, there is no known fix for this issue, which affects products from leading manufacturers. As a result, researchers outlined potential workarounds and suggested further investigation is required to address this significant vulnerability. This weakness, which researchers dubbed "Protocol Ambiguity Attack" (PAAs),, can be triggered using straightforward methods including exploiting pre-existing system features and targeting specific vulnerabilities. Focusing on deep packet inspection (DPI) tools, researchers discovered the attack could alter traffic patterns in various ways including, but not limited to, forcing misidentification of SSH traffic as FTP traffic. Through various DPI tool tests, researchers discovered certain features can greatly increase an attacker's chances of success while others have little effect. As these findings apply broadly across many network systems, researchers concluded that network operators should be aware of these vulnerabilities and take steps to mitigate the threat. Additionally, researchers discussed the potential use of cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generators as a potential fix, although this would not address the underlying flaw in these systems. In response to the coronavirus pandemic, many news sources revived their print editions or transitioned to online platforms, with some regions receiving more coverage than others. This research targets regional news outlets in the U.S., examining their online presence, audience size, COVID-related cases and deaths, and how these factors are interconnected. The results are supported by statistical analysis and case studies from four areas: New York, Texas, California, and Florida. Crucially, this study reveals how regional news outlets influence their local communities' awareness of COVID-related data, showcasing a causal relationship between news coverage, audience size, and COVID statistics. Moreover, the research confirms that larger news platforms have a greater impact on the discussion around COVID data. By simulating different scenarios, the research shows that increased news coverage can lead to a greater proportion of the population discussing COVID-related topics. Based on these findings, the research puts forth several theoretical implications that can be applied to the study of social media and news environments. Ultimately, the research provides insight into the interconnectedness of news, social influence, and COVID statistics, and offers a framework for the systematic study of these complex systems. This work presents FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework, designed to 
ensure and maintain user privacy. FLVoogd combines significant features from 
previous research and incorporates two primary contributions: (1) 
confinement-based regularization and (2) a confidence-based pruning technique. 
Both mechanisms contribute to enhancing the learning process and mitigating 
overfitting, all while upholding the principles of federated learning. Our 
evaluation showcases the effectiveness of FLVoogd through clear, visible results, 
and its code is freely accessible via the corresponding GitHub repository. 
Furthermore, the theoretical underpinnings of FLVoogd's performance are 
investigated, highlighting its excellence relative to state-of-the-art FL models. 
Given its decentralization, ease of use, and high performance, FLVoogd is an 
excellent choice for complex computer-vision applications, and we envision its 
広範囲的 adoption in the federated learning community. Our study also offers 
valuable insights on the trade-offs inherent in federated learning. The primary 
advantage of FLVoogd lies in its ability to strike a balance between model 
performance and privacy, thereby circumventing the traditional 'hairball' issue. 
In contrast to existing research, we do not seek to optimize either aspect; 
stead, we explore the intermediate region, and this unique approach enables us 
to delve into the inherent complexities of federated learning. The companion 
artificial intelligence model, AIVoogd, is also presented as a general ML model, 
and it exhibits unparalleled performance compared to leading competition in 
tackling the 2022 ImageNet competition. The remarkable AIVoogd is a 
consequence of the Federated Learning paradigm employed during its training. This 
artificial intelligence model exemplifies a novel approach in ML, where we 
redefine overfitting as a local overfitting and global overfitting issue, and 
Mitigate both through regularization and pruning, effectively combating the 
sustained pursuit of ultimate generalization. This groundbreaking redefinition 
and novel approach will surely have a profound impact on the natural language 
community, and we envision its widespread adoption in the future. Lastly, our 
framework and model AIVoogd are designed with user privacy and data protection 
in mind, in accordance with the evolving standards of the European General 
Data Protection Regulation. This privacy-focused approach is in line with the 
ongoing efforts to integrate fluoroscopy-based federated learning

Significant and harmful deepfakes have sparked a rush to develop both creation and detection techniques, primarily centered on professional settings and limited by constraints such as single-source identities, bounded pixel ranges, and restricted resolution limits. In response to deepfakes' vast potential for harm, there's an increasing need for more versatile approaches that are both harder to create and detect, especially in everyday media. This research closes the gap by developing highly effective techniques for both creating and spotting deepfakes in everyday videos, despite and partly due to their ease of manufacture, essentially leaving room for only marginally superior attackers. Unlike previous methods, our approach doesn't rely on restrictive assumptions and is instead grounded in the fundamental building blocks of deepfake detection, revealing an unexpected trade-off between creating and detecting deepfakes. This understanding has allowed us to develop new strategies that significantly outperform previous methods in unconstrained media, ultimately exposing an unexpected connection between face verification and deepfake detection, and opening new avenues for future research. Our creation method showcases the ease of manufacturing highly convincing deepfakes in everyday videos, detected by our highly effective and powerful detection method, which significantly outperforms previous methods, also providing valuable insights into deepfake detection, and facilitating face verification task solutions. Our code and unconstrained deepfake video dataset are available for free at https://github.com/b-5-4/UDF. This research has been accepted for publication at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023.

The discovery of exoplanets with masses similar to those of Neptune has led to advancements in the study of gas giant formation and the evaluation of remote sensing methods for identifying hidden substellar atmospheres. To this aim, we are investigating whether specific spectral features can distinguish between solutions of soluble gases and thermal models, using numerical simulations based on a 2D energy balance model that incorporates soluble gas equilibrium. Key markers of soluble gas solutions include a paucity of molecular absorption in the near-infrared and observable ozone absorption at 750 nm. A model paucity of water absorption around 1.4 $\mu$m also characterizes soluble gas solutions. Characterizing a soluble gas atmosphere is feasible through a single transit observation, particularly if the planet orbits a late-type star with high metallicity, as indicated by spectroscopic analysis. If verified, this approach could enable the identification of substellar atmospheres with soluble gases in the solar neighborhood, potentially followed by the application of remote sensing methods to detect concealed oceans. A key advantage of this method over existing paucity of water techniques lies in its reduced reliance on host star metallicity. Furthermore, this approach may facilitate the detection of more massive objects, such as Neptunes, due to higher signal-to-noise ratios during transits. Based on these estimates, a detectable soluble gas solution could be expected for up to 4.5% of nearby Neptune-mass planets with compositions similar to those of Uranus and Neptune, as well as for a substantially higher fraction, approximately 20.3%, if we consider more massive massive gas giants, such as those with masses up to 10 M$_{\earth}$. To explore these possibilities, we are proposing a targeted observing campaign using the Very Large Telescope and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Infrared Spectrograph. A successful outcome would significantly broaden the scope of remote sensing methods, ultimately leading to the detection and characterization of concealed substellar atmospheres, as well as those supporting liquid water and life. Additionally, this approach may facilitate the preparation for the detection and characterization of exoplanets with observable soluble gas solutions during the James Webb Space Telescope era. To lay the groundwork for these efforts, we are estimating the frequency of soluble gas solutions in the solar neighborhood, as well as those supporting liquid water, based on existing and proposed observational data. As a result, even though the planet orbiting the late-type star with the highest metallicity proves to be a gas giant rather than a Neptune, this approach remains viable for detecting hidden oceans in the solar neighborhood

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain parameters by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. However, verifying the accuracy of these expansions requires computing an error estimate related to a norm of the residual in the original differential equation. In this study, we present a method that makes it possible to calculate this error estimate without simulating the entire differential equation process, thereby facilitating the computation of the error, particularly for complicated processes. A demonstration of this approach is provided through a numerical analysis of a generalized polynomial chaos expansion that solves a second-order differential equation with a ball in three-dimensional space. The main limitations of the proposed method are then discussed. This approach can be adapted for use with other chaos expansions and is compatible with pre-existing simulation tools. Furthermore, the code used in this study has been made available online for reference. A possible future direction of this research involves generalizing the approach to analyze partial differential equations with multiple dimensions. Additionally, the main limitation of the method is related to its reliance on solution trajectories, which could be overcome through the use of the method of fundamental solutions. Therefore, this study also investigates the possibility of using this approach in conjunction with the method of fundamental solutions.

The goal in the adaptive partially-observed sequential change identification and isolation problem is to detect and separate sequences of varying lengths that have been selected from a larger database, taking into account a pre-defined threshold for acceptance. Both the training and test sequences are subject to partial observation, where a portion of the sequence is masked. To solve this problem, an advanced algorithm and its theoretical proof have been developed, demonstrating that the number of false positives and false negatives can be bounded by a factor of o(n^-c), where c is a positive constant less than 1, under specific conditions. Furthermore, the variance of the estimated error rates is shown to converge to a value greater than 1, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first such result in a partial observation setting. Additionally, the influence of the degree of partial observation on the algorithm's performance has been studied experimentally. Results from these experiments suggest that the algorithm's performance remains robust to changes in the level of partial observation. A variant of the algorithm that incorporates the use of partial colors has also been proposed, this adaptation aims to mitigate the negative impact of partial observation on the algorithm's performance, while also providing a more accurate estimation of the sequences' beginnings. The efficacy of this adaptation was confirmed through experimental testing. Both algorithms have been implemented in a publicly-available Python package, named aposis, that is designed to facilitate the use of these techniques in a wide range of applications. The package provides a flexible tool for detecting and isolating sequences of varying lengths in a database, even when they are partially observed. Additionally, the package includes an extended version of the algorithm that incorporates the use of partial colors. The aposis package is compatible with Jupyter Notebooks and can be used in a variety of applications, including audio analysis. A comprehensive guide to the package is included in the documentation. The source code for the package is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/ahmedrafaat/aposis. This research was conducted while the lead author was a visiting student at the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. It has been presented at the 2021 Microsoft Coffee and Viz meeting and the 2022 Cambridge Machine Learning Meetup. A preliminary version of this work was published in the arXiv database under the title "Partially-Observed Sequential Change Identification and Isolation", it has since received two reviews, both of which have led to revisions that have improved the paper's clarity and completeness. The revised paper has now been accepted for publication

We have created a comprehensive dataset of the metal content, size, and star formation history for 57 dwarf galaxies from various studies and compared it to the simulation results of two distinct models of star formation and chemical evolution. The difference in predictions from these models is relatively small, but it's particularly distinct in the case of low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. The challenge of accurately replicating the enrichment of heavy elements in low-metallicity dwarf galaxies has led to a long-standing issue in the field. Although the models agree that hydrogen turns into helium through simple nuclear reactions, the process of creating heavier elements requires complex astrophysical calculations and simulations often include explosive events like supernovae and winds from massive stars. By comparing the predicted metal content and star formation histories to the actual values from observed dwarf galaxies, we were able to determine the optimal parameters for two key processes: the efficiency with which matter is expelled from stars and the maximum amount of heavy elements that can be created before a star explodes, turning its metal content into the surrounding space. Document analysis, a field that has been around for decades, is relatively underfunded compared to other areas of computer vision. The cost of annotating these documents can be prohibitive, making it even more difficult to find funding. Our proposed method allows us to transfer knowledge from existing, publicly available datasets, significantly reducing the need for manual labeling. By doing so, we can also select the most useful labels and prioritize annotation for areas such as layout detection, reducing the costs associated with extracting a full set of labels for every document. Our approach allows us to train a dataset with just 10% of the labels from a different, visually rich dataset, replacing a set of expertly crafted labels for the dataset SegVOC. The results show that our transfer learning strategy is successful, with our model achieving near-perfect performance on the SegVOC dataset after being trained on the publicly available COCO-Stuff dataset. Additionally, we found that layout detection can be perfectly predicted by a model trained on the COCO-StOC dataset with just 10% of SegVOC labels, outperforming a model trained on SegVOC with expertly annotated labels. These findings have significant practical implications, allowing us to bypass the high costs associated with annotating labels for complex document analysis. Our code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ultralytics/segvoc. The paper has been accepted for Orals at CVPR 2022. Despite recent advances in neural network pruning, most current approaches still limit the depth of their layer stacks and/or the width of their model structures to facilitate pruning. This is because previous methods typically employ task-specific training after a general model is trained, a process that necessitates a layer to be skipped. We propose clicktrain, a novel universal framework for both training and pruning deep neural networks without these constraints. The framework employs a decoding process that retains the original model's depth and includes a multi-grained pruning strategy, allowing for the adjustment of parameters at the layer, channel, and neuron levels. The framework is engineered to maintain the original model's structure and has been successfully applied to various tasks across computer vision and natural language processing, yielding state-of-the-art results. The framework's source code is available at https://github.com/He-Mao/ClickTrain. Experiments demonstrate that clicktrain, when applied to ResNet-50, allows for a model size reduction of up to 80.6% with no decrease in top-1 accuracy, from 0.794 to 0.794. Additionally, clicktrain has been used to prune ResNet-50, increasing the top-1 accuracy of Accetto, a model trained on the ImageNet dataset, from 0.794 to 0.847, representing a 6.3% improvement in accuracy, all with a model size reduction of 80.6%. Building upon this breakthrough, the detection of gravitational waves from neutron star-black hole collisions, such as S200024n, has enabled new avenues for exploration. With the growing repertoire of gravitational wave events, the challenge now lies in efficiently classifying them based on increasingly limited signal data. Traditional methods, which were effective for the initial detections, now struggle to classify the more recent, weaker signals with varying levels of noise. To address this issue, we employ deep learning techniques, including convolutional neural networks and generative adversarial networks, to identify and categorize the compact binary systems. Our study utilizes the analysis of 113 real and simulated gravitational waves, spanning three categories: binary black hole, neutron star-black hole, and binary black hole with intermediate mass ratios. The findings, however, reveal that the distinction between neutron star-black hole and binary black hole systems is not supported. Furthermore, we investigate the efficacy of our methods when applied to the analysis of individual components, such as peaking amplitude and signal duration. Our work, while driven by the study of compact binary systems, has broader implications and can be extended to various applications in gravitational wave research and other multi-messenger paradigms. The code and gravitational wave data used for this study are publicly available at https://github.com/hydata/gwtune/tree/main/DeepLearning and https://grizzly.gwtunes.org/. Our analysis also utilizes the LALInference package, whose extensive library of simulated events has been a invaluable resource for this study. The final version of this paper has been published in Physical Review D, with the DOI: 10.1103/PhysRevD.107.084065. We have also prepared a review on this topic, which can be found at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.48531/2022.06511. We develop a primal-dual method to solve complex optimization problems involving sequences of Markov decision processes. By employing a novel primal-dual algorithm, we derive nearly optimal solutions for a broad class of such optimization problems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we showcase its application in addressing two intractable problems: a model for optimizing resource allocation and a method for solving constrained bandit problems. Empirical evidence reveals that our primal-dual method yields high-quality solutions that significantly outperform alternative solutions obtained through alternative techniques. Crucially, we prove that the computational burden associated with each iteration of our primal-dual method grows polynomially with problem size. To achieve this polynomial complexity, we employ a family of constrained Markov choice procedures, whose existence has so far been contingent on the Lasserre hierarchy upper bounds. We overcome this limitation by establishing a novel proof based on a graph expansion technique. Our primal-dual method can also be specialized to yield near-optimal solutions for a range of stand-alone Markov decision problems, including optimizing codebook formation and data compression. We provide a thorough set of experimental results that illustrate the efficacy of our approach. Our algorithm's code is available online at https://github.com/aimlabmit/primal-dual-mcp. This research outlines a method for offline handwritten mathematical formula recognition using deep learning. The approach relies on a large dataset of ground-edited mathematical expressions, which serves as both training and validation tools. A pre-trained, modular architecture for mathematical symbol recognition is then fine-tuned to recognize entire formulas. Additionally, we describe a pipeline that generates proposed recognition models and evaluates their accuracy on an extensive mathematical expression dataset. Our method was put to the test on the Math, IT and Finance Collection, which comprises 83,897 handwritten mathematical formulas, gathered from the marks of students in Lancaster University. Evaluation results demonstrate a substantial improvement in recognition accuracy with the deep learning model, which outperforms a previously employed method based on Penmanship and Connectionism. Moreover, we discovered a significant increase in the overall correctness of proposed recognition models over a baseline method, achieving very high accuracy rates of 97.7% on the training and 94.3% on the test sets. Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that orbits within the Adams Ring system, has been found to have a surface composed of water ice. Research has now been conducted using data from the New Horizons spacecraft during its flyby of Nereid in 2014, which revealed significant variations in the surface reflectance of the satellite. These differences were observed across the 1.5 $\mu$m water ice absorption band, suggesting the presence of various ices. To further investigate these findings, modeling of the reflectance spectra has been undertaken using a physical model that takes into account the size and composition of the satellite's surface features. This analysis indicates that Nereid's ice crystals could be comprised of about 60% water ice, with the remaining 40% consisting of other volatiles such as ammonia, carbon dioxide, or methane ice. The evidence for carbon dioxide ice on Nereid, in particular, is considered to be the most compelling of these possibilities. The composition of Nereid's surface ice is thought to be the result of past colisions between the satellite and objects in the Adams Ring system, which have transferred volatile compounds to the satellite's surface. The presence of CO$_2$ ice on Nereid, in turn, indicates that these halides could also be found in the surfaces of other objects in the Adams Ring system, such as Halimede and Praxitlis. The findings of this study, in particular, highlight the potential of optical spectroscopy, rather than thermal infrared spectroscopy, in the analysis of extragalactic icy surfaces at close range. The observation of Nereid's surface also revealed variations in texture and composition that cannot be explained by the simple water ice model that was initially employed. The presence of areas with clear water ice, as well as areas with "chaotic" ice that are similar in appearance to those found on the Jupiter moon, Hyperion, were both identified. The proposed theory can be extended to involve multiple bosons and is applicable to a range of systems including the graphene moiré heterostructure. We demonstrate that under specific conditions, the superconducting gap structure predicted by a theory involving one boson is replicated with higher-gapped multiples of this gap occurring. However, this replication is not seen in all flat-topology systems; specific graphene and carbonene systems exhibit replica gaps at multiples of the primary gap, whereas these replica gaps are only seen in one component of the heterostructure gap. Our findings can be experimentally verified by the assessment of gap nodal structures and by the observation of multiple phase transitions. The proposed theory also predicts that when multiple boson pairs form simultaneously in different bands, these pairs will couple to produce a higher-gapped multiple of the primary gap in each individual band. The primary boson pairs will also couple across bands to produce higher-gapped multiples of the primary gap in the combined system. The specific higher-gapped multiples seen in both the individual and combined systems can be explained by a general equation for multiple boson coupling. Comparing clustering methods such as k-means, hierarchical clustering, and others showed that none of them outperformed the other across all data sets. When data dimensionality is high and cluster sizes are unequal, a novel approach proved effective in identifying distinct groups. Notably, the study found that: (1) incorporating variance normalization significantly improved clustering results; (2) under-sampled data tended to receive better cluster assignments than densely sampled data; (3) certain clustering methods performed better on data with missing values than those with complete data; (4) using an unbiased metric preferred larger clusters over smaller ones; (5) evaluating cluster compactness and distribution separately from purity improved the identification of distinct groups. The researchers also introduced a calibration process to analyze the shape of data distributions, providing more accurate estimates of cluster sizes and shapes. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with objects of various sizes remains a significant challenge.  Object-based approaches  have been proposed to overcome this challenge, but they often rely on pre-defined object boundaries, which are difficult to obtain.  An alternative solution, called the Fully Convolutional Network (FCN), focuses on learning a full-scale map to achieve this goal.  However, determining an effective scale for the FCN is crucial.  A scale transfer learning framework is proposed to address this challenge by transferring scale information from the input image to the saliency map.  An optimal scale extraction module is designed to extract a representative scale from the input image.  An adaptive dilated convolution module is then employed to fuse multi-scale features effectively.  Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.  A comparison with 8 recent state-of-the-art methods on 4 datasets shows that our method performs significantly better.  Also, a discussion on the impact of dilated convolution on saliency detection is included.  Importantly, the proposed framework is universally applicable to various RGB and RGB-D salient object detection methods.  An implementation in PyTorch is available at https://github.com/Stanley-Stanley/UN4S.  Extensive experiments on 4 public datasets reveal that 8 recent state-of-the-art methods integrated with our framework achieve better performance.  Additionally, an ablation study confirms the effectiveness of our framework.  Specifically, the results on the MSRA-Boundies dataset show a significant performance boost of 6.76% and 10.82% for RGB and RGB-D scenarios respectively.  Also, the results on the Aachen dataset show a significant performance boost of 13.53% and 20.46% for RGB and RGB-D scenarios respectively.  These impressive performance boosts indicate that our framework is a valuable integration method.  Also, the fact that it is universally applicable to various existing methods further confirms its significance.  Therefore, we expect that our framework will be widely adopted in the field of saliency detection.  Also, we plan to test its effectiveness on more datasets in the future. Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves combining measurements from diverse sensors. Inspired by recent breakthroughs in convex variational reconstruction methods, this study presents an innovative non-convex approach to CT image reconstruction that accounts for the simultaneous effects of gradient-index sensing and polyenergetic X-rays, in addition to material decomposition. We develop a customized variational framework, supplemented by exact and approximate preconditioners that facilitate efficient image reconstruction. The technique's efficacy is demonstrated through the reconstruction of CT scans using artificially generated and real-world data. Results indicate that the proposed method outperforms standard techniques in terms of reconstructions accuracy and quality. The algorithm's source code is available for free on GitHub at https://github.com/andersonchagas/PolyCT.andy.

To address this, we've developed an approach called Single-shot Compositional Data Creation (SCDC), which generates synthetic texts by manipulating real text samples into unfamiliar scripts, then reverses them to their original forms using an unsupervised language model. Since this process relies on scripts rather than text segments, it remains unfamiliar to the model. Moreover, we've successfully applied SCDC to a real-world dataset obtained from an Indian museum's record books, thereby facilitating accurate recognition of ancient documents. A novel approach called "Combined Ab Initio Computations" has been developed to simultaneously calculate the positions of atoms in solids and the energies associated with atomic interactions.  This methodology incorporates a novel tight-binding based method that accurately predicts the interatomic potentials necessary for accurate simulations of atomic interactions.  Three distinct TB models were constructed for the case of palladium using experimental data: the "Minimum Atomic Basis Set" which relies on first-order TB models for weak and van der Waals interactions, and two second-order TB models that utilize Feynman's classical path approximation and a high-frequency representation.  These TB models were then used to determine the energy landscape of palladium through the use of a finite-temperature perturbation theory, and were further applied to model the thermal expansion of the metal.  Our calculations demonstrate that the application of the perturbation theory and the consideration of multiple electron excitations, in addition to the exchange-correlation energy, are essential for the accurate modeling of atomic interactions. Through a detailed analysis, we demonstrate the development of topological quantum numbers as well as various structural characteristics within the eigenspectrum. As a key contribution, we establish a protocol for identifying concepts, particularly topological ones, in the eigenenergy count or eigenvalue distribution. High-performance computing on GPUs significantly boosts the performance of object-oriented programs, but this is contingent on efficient memory allocation. However, the standard memory allocator used in C-like languages does not take into account the specific access patterns involved in GPU programming, which can lead to significant slowdowns. In an effort to address this issue, we have developed a novel memory allocator, referred to as DynaSOAr. This allocator is designed to optimize memory usage on GPUs by simultaneously placing objects of different sizes in memory. We evaluated the performance of DynaSOAr by comparing it to a range of other allocators, including both sequential and parallel models. Our results indicate that DynaSOAr is capable of allocating memory at least 30% faster while maintaining the same level of correctness. Furthermore, we observed a maximum speedup of 2.3 times higher memory allocation speed with DynaSOAr. To further refine the performance of DynaSOAr, we are releasing the algorithm as open-source software. Our research also reveals that there are only three possible methods for allocating memory in a parallel environment, and we prove the correctness of DynaSOAr using the Banicear theorem. We also provide an analysis of the time and space complexity of DynaSOAr. Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr consistently outperforms other allocators by a substantial margin, and we identify an optimal configuration for the allocator. Our findings also indicate that a parallel memory allocation system with an internal memory size equal to half the GPU's total memory and a block size equal to 64 bytes is the most efficient configuration. Moreover, we observed that DynaSOAr is capable of allocating memory at a rate of over 1 GB per millisecond on a modern GPU. Our research offers several areas for future research, including the development of parallel memory allocation systems in languages other than C. Our work also addresses a notable gap in the literature by providing a comprehensive theoretical framework and practical algorithm for parallel memory allocation. Our research provides a valuable contribution to the field by offering an efficient and widely applicable solution to the problem. Our findings can be useful to programmers, researchers, and developers working with object-oriented programs who are seeking to enhance the performance of their code using GPUs. Our research may also spur the development of new techniques and algorithms for parallel memory allocation. Our findings can be applied to other domains beyond high-performance computing, including real-time systems and embedded programming. Therefore, extracting key features from the incoming data streams is crucial for classifying these devices efficiently. However, selecting the optimal set of features is a complex task, particularly when working with a large number of features and uncertain device capabilities. To address this issue, we developed a novel technique that identifies the most valuable features for classification purposes, taking into account the computational costs involved. Our approach relies on a two-step process that first uses a genetic algorithm to identify the optimal feature subset, and then uses a clustering method to evaluate the importance of each feature within those subsets. Additionally, we introduced two new methods for predicting the classification performance of new data samples based on past device activity. These techniques can be used independently or combined as follows: (1) The Future classifier: a future sample predictor that uses past data from the same device; (2) The Leader classifier: a leader classifier that connects to the top classifier of each connected device. Our methods were validated by conducting experiments on real-world datasets, and our evaluation shows that they achieve better classification performance while reducing computational costs compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. However, as these systems evolve, their total volume in phase space remains constant, posing a significant challenge. Understanding how this challenge affects systems going through free expansion provides valuable insights into its dynamics. In this study, we present an innovative approach to investigate this issue, focusing on the thermodynamic properties of a system undergoing free expansion. By applying a Hamiltonian transformation, we're able to eliminate the system's time-dependent behavior and compare its initial and final states directly. This new approach enables us to determine the system's microstate density without being confounded by time-dependent correlations. Furthermore, we develop a method for modeling the system's behavior using a time-evolving Hamiltonian. This, in turn, allows us to determine the system's initial phase space volume, thus resolving a long-standing issue associated with quantizing systems with varying phase space volumes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this new technique by applying it to simulations of monatomic argon gas and even identify the system's first principle thermal expansion. By combining this new technique with Monte Carlo methods, we're able to determine the system's energy distribution and develop a novel approach to estimating thermodynamic properties. This includes determining thermodynamic properties solely based on the system's energy distribution, thereby bypassing the need for time-dependent corrections. As a result, we're able to calculate thermodynamic properties with enhanced precision and predict the system's behavior under different thermal conditions. Ultimately, this new approach, which we call MICROS, facilitates calculating thermodynamic properties and predicting the system's behavior without requiring a thermodynamic parameter. By applying it to a wide range of systems, we're confident it can revolutionize the way we perform computational thermodynamics. Since its underlying principles are applicable to a broad range of problems, we're prepared to extend its usage to many other systems and research fields. It's also worth mentioning that one of the key concepts of this new approach - eliminating time-dependent correlations - can be applied independently of the specific algorithms used to simulate the system's behavior. Therefore, we're confident that the techniques presented here can be applied to a broad range of algorithms to solve the challenges posed by time-dependent correlations. Finally, we're hopeful that the new approach outlined in this work will inspire new ideas in the field of computational thermodynamics. It's particularly suited to systems that undergo changes in volume, but we're confident it can be applied to a broader range of problems as well. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 has been studied with a series of Bi-doped samples. We examined how the band gap size, affecting metallic or insulating behavior, changes with increasing Bi content. We used hard X-ray photoemission spectroscopy to investigate the band structure, and observed that varying Bi content leads to a continuous insulator-to-metal transition without detecting any intermediate phases. We relate this transition to the alteration in average spin moment caused by Bi doping, specifically a decrease with increasing Bi content, and employ band structure computations to validate our findings. We further discuss how the insulator-to-metal shift in (Eu, Bi)2Ir2O7 can be explained through a hybridization gap size that correlates directly with the local magnetic character of the cation orbitals. This discovery opens a wider range of possibilities for controlling the electronic properties of the pyrochlore iridates family through doping. We also discovered evidence of electron correlation in the Bi-doped samples, particularly in the d-like emission peak, and observed an increase in correlation-related energy splitting with rising Bi content. We further examine various phenomena often associated with Weyl semimetals, such as edge states and ferromagnetic ordering, in the (Eu, Bi)2Ir2O7 series, and discuss how these effects are impacted by Bi doping. Notably, we discovered that Bi doping causes the reduction of edge state-related energy and the gap at the Fermi level related to magnetic ordering, leading to the potential emergence of a zero-gap state. Most current statistical models necessitate setting several parameters, often through expensive, time-consuming processes, especially in complex scenarios. A key objective is to automate this parameter setting, often referred to as 'hyper-parameter optimization.' In machine learning, for example, finding the ideal balance between different models is crucial and is typically achieved by optimizing parameters like model size and learning speed. Advances in both neural networks and other statistical models have created a pressing need to streamline this process. Recent breakthroughs involving, for example, transfer learning and pre-trained models indicate that one fruitful approach is to specialize in specific areas of the parameter space in advance, a concept known as'meta-parameters.' A promising possibility is to use information available at compile-time (e.g. code structure, developer intentions) to influence parameters set at run-time. A potential innovation would be to use multi-context graph networks to correlate compile-time factors with optimal run-time settings, a notion explored in this study. Using a realistic case involving text classification, this study demonstrates that such an approach, while speculative, has a solid foundation and is worth further research. Measuring the inter-beat interval (IBI) in electrocardiograms (ECG) is crucial for analyzing heart rhythms and detecting specific conditions such as heart disorders. However, identifying IBI from raw ECG signals is an intricate process due to potential errors. In this research, a novel method employing a Tiramisu model is proposed to enhance IBI identification accuracy by mitigating errors. Initially, pre-processing is performed to refine the raw signal, and then feature extraction is conducted to optimize data representation. Subsequent R-squared calculations evaluate the reliability of features, followed by classification to determine the IBI. Finally, a post-processing step involving a Tiramisu model, trained on a large dataset with R-squared values, produces the final IBI readings. The proposed Tiramisu model, powered by a custom loss function, leverages channel-wise parameters and feature maps to achieve optimal results. The proposed approach, featuring a unique multi-branch architecture, allows for feature extraction and classification within a single network, thereby reducing computation and error. Comprehensive studies on diverse datasets demonstrate the outstanding performance of the proposed method over existing Tiramisu models and other prominent deep learning techniques. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of pre- and post-processing steps on error rates, showcasing the importance of these stages in accurate IBI identification. Lastly, the proposed method is assessed in terms of its reliability, patient selection criteria, and clinical applicability, highlighting its potential for heart rhythm disorder detection and diagnosis. The proposed research not only contributes to the field but also paves the way for further exploration into the role of pre- and post-processing in deep learning models in the context of electrocardiogram analysis. The source code for the proposed approach has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/kkranthi90/Tiramisu_IBI_RSD. Additionally, the pre-trained models and associated datasets can be accessed via GitHub at https://github.com/kkranthi90/Tiramisu_IBI_RSD/blob/master/data.zip. Despite the vast amount of data and advanced technology in natural language processing, many useful tasks remain unsolved for certain languages due to a lack of data. A promising solution to this problem is model-independent cross-lingual transfer, where knowledge from a well-documented language is applied to a less documented one. Typically, this approach requires detailed task definitions and precise feature mappings between languages, a difficult and often unsatisfiable condition. We propose a feeble supervision method that eliminates these requirements, instead representing tasks through neural models trained on unlabeled data. We put this idea to the test by applying it to parts-of-speech tagging tasks across six languages, and found that our approach surpasses previous methods, achieving high accuracy on tasks with no existing labels. It is possible for similar models to be developed for other tasks, such as machine translation and sentiment analysis, potentially unlocking new applications for under-resourced languages. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/samaborders/feeblexlt.
